Application of Matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry in rapid identification and antimicrobial susceptibility testing of bacterial bloodstream infections
abstract: Abstract Background Bloodstream infection (BSI) is a severe common clinical infection, without timely intervention, the infection may progress to sepsis and increase the risk of mortality in patients.MALDI- TOF MS can rapidly identify pathogens directly from positive blood cultures. However, few systematic evaluations have assessed MALDI- TOF MS combined with rapid antimicrobial susceptibility testing (RAST) for positive blood cultures. Evidence regarding identification accuracy among different pathogens, agreement between RAST and conventional susceptibility testing, and clinical value remains insufficient. This study compared the performance of direct MALDI- TOF MS identification with conventional methods, analyzed the concordance between RAST and routine susceptibility results, and explored the diagnostic value of this combined workflow for bacterial BSI, aiming to shorten turnaround time and support antimicrobial stewardship. Methods From January 2024 to August 2026, 428 positive blood cultures were collected from the Microbiology Laboratory of Guangzhou Red Cross Hospital. Pathogens were enriched via high- speed centrifugation sedimentation for direct MALDI- TOF MS identification. Monomicrobial positive broths underwent RAST following EUCAST guidelines, with susceptibility readouts at 4 h, 6 h and 8 h. Subcultured colony MALDI- TOF MS identification and VITEK 2 Compact susceptibility results served as references to assess concordance. Results Among 428 isolates, 295 Gram- negative bacilli showed 91.5% identification concordance; 28 Gram- positive bacilli 78.6%; 105 Gram- positive cocci 82.9%. RAST analysis included 279 specimens. Categorical agreement (CA) rose with incubation time. For Enterobacterales, CA exceeded 90% for most antibiotics at 8 h. Gram- positive cocci yielded poor growth at 4 h precluding inhibition zone measurement, while concordance improved markedly at 8 h. Conclusion MALDI- TOF MS combined with RAST achieves rapid, reasonably accurate pathogen identification and preliminary susceptibility testing for positive blood cultures. The 8- hour susceptibility results have good clinical utility and can guide early antibiotic selection in BSI patients.

title: Efficacy of vibroacoustic chest massage in patients with community-acquired pneumonia
abstract: Aim: to evaluate the clinical outcomes of vibroacoustic chest massage used as part of respiratory rehabilitation in patients with community-acquired pneumonia treated in a critical care setting. Materials and methods. This prospective randomized comparative study included 100 patients with community-acquired pneumonia treated in the resuscitation and intensive care unit. The median age was 56 [45,6; 67,5] years; the study population included 36 men and 64 women. Patients were randomized into two groups. The vibroacoustic massage group (n = 50; 13 men and 37 women) received standard comprehensive therapy for community-acquired pneumonia and correction of respiratory failure, including incentive spirometry, CPAP therapy, respiratory activation, and low-flow oxygen therapy; these measures were supplemented by vibroacoustic chest massage sessions. The control group (n = 50; 23 men and 27 women) received standard comprehensive therapy for community-acquired pneumonia and correction of respiratory failure without vibroacoustic massage. The study endpoints were in-hospital treatment parameters, including the length of stay in the resuscitation and intensive care unit and total hospital stay, the need for invasive mechanical ventilation, sanitation fibrobronchoscopy, changes in antibacterial therapy, and the dynamics of oxygenation parameters. Results. During the stay in the resuscitation and intensive care unit, invasive mechanical ventilation was required in 8 patients in the vibroacoustic massage group and in 6 patients in the control group; the differences were not statistically significant. By the third session, oxygen saturation in the vibroacoustic massage group differed significantly from that in the control group. The dynamics of the PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio were the most pronounced: starting from the second day of observation, statistically significant differences were observed in favor of the vibroacoustic massage group. Conclusions. Course-based use of vibroacoustic chest massage as part of respiratory rehabilitation in patients with community-acquired pneumonia treated in a critical care setting was associated with improvement in selected in-hospital outcomes, including a shorter total hospital stay and a lower need for sanitation fibrobronchoscopy.

title: Fontan patients with systemic left ventricle have superior response to 6-month exercise program over patients with right ventricle
abstract: OBJECTIVES: In Fontan patients, transpulmonary flow depends on systemic venous pressure, pulmonary vascular resistance, and ventricle preload. Reduction in cardiopulmonary function is common in Fontan patients. Exercise is considered a promising self-care method to harden particularly lower limbs for supporting transpulmonary flow. We studied whether a 6-month exercise program improves cardiopulmonary function in Fontan patients and if the response is dependent on ventricular morphology. Before the individualised self-guided training, the test subjects were inquired for exercise habits followed by cardiopulmonary exercise testing, body composition, and muscular fitness. Repeat testing was done in 31 patients that completed the exercise prescription. Differences between groups were tested using one-way analysis of variance; within-group changes were analysed using paired t-tests. RESULTS: = 0.009). RV-R subgroup demonstrated a reduction in the VE/VCO₂ slope, indicating improved ventilation-perfusion matching. Pulmonary function remained unchanged. Muscular fitness improved across all groups. CONCLUSION: A home-based 6-month exercise program was safe and functional. Patients with systemic LV demonstrated superior improvements in cardiopulmonary fitness. Patients with hypoplastic left heart (RV morphology) improved ventilatory efficiency only. Differences in coronary perfusion may affect exercise response in hypoplastic left heart syndrome.

title: Effects of Transurethral Thulium Laser Enucleation of the Prostate on Postoperative Erectile Function and Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms in Patients With Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia
abstract: BACKGROUND This prospective randomized study examined whether transurethral thulium laser enucleation of the prostate (THuLEP) provides greater early improvement in lower urinary tract symptoms than transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) and compared secondary perioperative and functional outcomes in patients with benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). MATERIAL AND METHODS A total of 104 patients with BPH treated from January 2021 to June 2023 were randomly assigned to TURP (n=52) or THuLEP (n=52). Primary outcome was 1-month postoperative between-group difference in International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS). Secondary outcomes included perioperative parameters, quality of life (QOL), International Index of Erectile Function-5 (IIEF-5), maximum urine flow rate (Qmax), postvoid residual volume (PVR), and 30-day complications. Sex hormone levels and inflammatory biomarkers interleukin-4 (IL-4) and IL-17 were evaluated as exploratory correlates of early postoperative status. RESULTS At 1 month, the primary endpoint favored THuLEP: mean IPSS was 5.35 ± 0.54 in the THuLEP group and 7.65±0.78 in the TURP group (unadjusted mean difference [THuLEP minus TURP], -2.30; 95% CI, -2.56 to -2.04; adjusted ß=-1.24; 95% CI, -1.68 to -0.80; P<0.01). Secondary analyses showed lower blood loss, shorter catheterization duration and hospital stay, higher 1-month IIEF-5 and Qmax, lower PVR and QOL, and fewer 30-day complications with THuLEP. Exploratory biomarker analyses showed 1-month between-group differences in E2, T, T/E2, IL-4, and IL-17. These early postoperative comparisons do not establish medium- or long-term superiority. CONCLUSIONS THuLEP produced a greater reduction in LUTS at 1 month than TURP for the prespecified primary endpoint. Several secondary perioperative and functional outcomes also favored THuLEP. Sexual-function and biomarker findings remain preliminary, requiring longer follow-up and external confirmation.

title: Esophageal-to-forehead zero-heat-flux temperature discrepancy during targeted temperature management as a predictor of brain death after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest
abstract: Continuous physiological surveillance of post-cardiac arrest brain injury remains a major clinical challenge. This study evaluated whether esophageal-to-forehead zero-heat-flux (ZHF) temperature discrepancy, measured non-invasively using ZHF technology, predicts brain death in real time among out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) survivors undergoing targeted temperature management (TTM). This prospective observational study enrolled adult comatose OHCA survivors treated with TTM between April 2021 and December 2025. Core temperature, measured with an esophageal probe, and zero-heat-flux forehead temperature (ZHF-FT), measured with a forehead non-thermo-flow sensor, were recorded hourly. The esophageal-to-forehead ZHF temperature discrepancy (∆T), defined as esophageal temperature minus ZHF-FT, was calculated as the average discrepancy over the full 24-hour TTM maintenance phase (∆T Main ). The primary outcome was brain death at discharge. Among 297 included patients, 45 (15.2%) progressed to brain death. During maintenance, mean ZHF-FT was significantly lower in the brain death group than in the non-brain death group (32.1 °C vs. 33.0 °C; p < 0.001), resulting in marked widening of ∆T Main (1.1 °C vs. 0.1 °C; p < 0.001). Area under the curve analysis demonstrated strong prognostic performance of ∆T Main for brain death (AUC 0.821). At a cut-off value of > 0.75 °C, specificity was 95.2% and the negative predictive value was 94.1%. In multivariable logistic regression, ∆T Main was independently associated with brain death (adjusted odds ratio 13.535; p < 0.001). A widened ∆T Main is a promising, independent, non-invasive bedside predictor of brain death at discharge, reflecting catastrophic hypoxic-ischemic brain injury and disrupted cerebral thermoregulation while providing an early window for donor management and resource allocation during the early post-resuscitation care period.

title: Factors Associated with In-Hospital Mortality in Adults with Generalized Secondary Peritonitis in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia: A Retrospective Cohort Study
abstract: Background Generalized secondary peritonitis is a life-threatening surgical emergency that demands prompt resuscitation, antimicrobial therapy, and effective source control. Evidence from resource-limited settings remains limited. This study describes the causes, clinical presentation, operative management, postoperative complications, and factors associated with in-hospital mortality among adults undergoing emergency laparotomy at a tertiary hospital in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. Methods We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of consecutive adults aged 18 years or older with intraoperatively confirmed generalized secondary peritonitis who underwent emergency laparotomy at St. Paul’s Hospital Millennium Medical College between September 2022 and August 2023. We extracted data from medical records, operative logbooks, surgical-site records, and discharge records. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality. Because only 20 deaths occurred, the multivariable model was restricted to two prespecified variables: preoperative systolic blood pressure below 90 mmHg and gangrenous small-bowel obstruction. We used Firth’s penalized logistic regression to reduce small-sample bias. The study is reported according to the Strengthening the Reporting of Cohort, Cross-sectional and Case-control Studies in Surgery (STROCSS) 2025 guideline. Results Of 186 eligible patients, 129 (69.4%) were male, and the median age was 28.5 years (interquartile range 22–38 years). Appendiceal perforation (57/186, 30.6%) and perforated peptic ulcer (43/186, 23.1%) were the leading causes, followed by gangrenous small-bowel obstruction (17/186, 9.1%), gangrenous sigmoid volvulus (15/186, 8.1%), and traumatic small-bowel perforation (14/186, 7.5%). At least one postoperative complication was recorded in 67 patients (36.0%; 95% confidence interval [CI] 29.4–43.1%). Twenty patients died in hospital, giving an in-hospital mortality of 10.8% (95% CI 6.7–15.2%). In exploratory penalized regression, preoperative systolic blood pressure below 90 mmHg (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] 5.42, 95% CI 1.82–16.14; p = 0.002) and gangrenous small-bowel obstruction (AOR 6.89, 95% CI 1.94–24.52; p = 0.003) were associated with higher odds of in-hospital mortality. Septic shock and multiorgan failure accounted for 85% of recorded immediate causes of death. Conclusions In this single-center cohort, generalized secondary peritonitis carried a substantial burden of postoperative morbidity and in-hospital mortality. Preoperative hypotension and gangrenous small-bowel obstruction were associated with higher odds of in-hospital mortality in exploratory analysis, though estimates were imprecise due to limited events. Larger multicenter studies with standardized severity and treatment-timing data are needed; these findings should not be interpreted as validated prediction rules.

title: Effect of emergency integrated traditional Chinese and Western medicine plus clinical nursing pathway in surgically-treated acute appendicitis patients
abstract: BACKGROUND Given the high risk of postoperative complications in patients undergoing surgery for acute appendicitis (AA), optimizing management methods is critical. AIM To elucidate the effects of emergency integrated traditional Chinese and Western medicine (ITCWM) combined with clinical nursing pathway (CNP) on surgical candidates for AA. METHODS A retrospective analysis was conducted on 130 individuals with AA requiring surgical intervention at Tianjin Nankai Hospital from September 2022 to September 2025. This cohort included 60 cases in the control group, which received routine nursing care, and 70 patients in the research group, who were treated with emergency ITCWM and CNP. Comparative analyses between the groups assessed several factors, including surgical recovery (time to bowel sound recovery, first flatus, ambulation, and length of hospital stay), postoperative pain (measured by the Numeric Rating Scale), mental state (Hamilton Depression/Anxiety Scale), sleep quality (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index), and complications (ileus, uroschesis, incision infection). RESULTS The data revealed a significantly shorter time to bowel sound recovery, first flatus, and ambulation, along with earlier hospital discharge and lower Numeric Rating Scale scores on postoperative days 1 and 3 in the research group compared to controls. Reductions in Hamilton Depression Scale, Hamilton Anxiety Scale, and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index scores were noted on the 1st and 3rd postoperative days, alongside a lower total complication rate (7.14% vs 20.00%). CONCLUSION The integration of emergency ITCWM and CNP demonstrates substantial advantages for AA patients requiring surgery, indicating a strong potential for clinical application.

title: Potential Synergistic Cardiotoxicity of Nab-Paclitaxel and Prior Anlotinib Therapy in a SMuRF-less Patient: A Case Report
abstract: Background Reports of acute myocardial infarction in patients without standard modifiable cardiovascular risk factors (SMuRF-less) continue to accumulate, and cancer treatment is one of the factors implicated in these events. Whether previous exposure to an anti-angiogenic agent changes the vascular response to a taxane given months later has received little attention. Case presentation A 63-year-old man with stage IV lung adenocarcinoma and EGFR and RET alterations, with no standard modifiable cardiovascular risk factor, received nab-paclitaxel 400 mg as a single agent. About 12 h later he developed chest tightness, dyspnoea and loss of consciousness, and spontaneous circulation returned after cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Electrocardiography showed ST-segment elevation in leads II, III and aVF. Coronary angiography showed acute occlusion at the ostium of the right coronary artery, and implantation of a drug-eluting stent restored TIMI 3 flow. His cumulative exposure to anlotinib before this admission was approximately 30 months, ending in August 2025. High-sensitivity cardiac troponin T rose from 816 to 909 pg/mL and D-dimer from 7.015 to 9.84 mg/L. He was discharged on day 16, and echocardiography seven weeks later showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 63%. Conclusions Nab-paclitaxel can be followed within hours by ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction in patients who carry no conventional risk factor, and long-standing preceding anti-angiogenic therapy may lower the threshold for such an event. Chest symptoms developing during or after taxane administration should not be attributed to hypersensitivity before an electrocardiogram has been obtained, and decisions about further anti-cancer treatment in this situation call for cardiology involvement.

title: Ketamine to treat depression and the wish to hasten death in advanced cancer patients: The KODIAC pilot study
abstract: Objectives To evaluate ketamine inpatients with advanced cancer, major depressive disorder (MDD) and wish to hasten death (WTHD). Methods Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (NCT04471818) in patients with advanced cancer receiving palliative care. Participants received standard antidepressant therapy and were randomized to ketamine or placebo. After 2 double-blind infusions, allocation was opened, and control patients could cross over to ketamine. The primary outcome was change in MDD according to the Mexican Brief Edinburgh Depression Scale (BEDS-Mx); WTHD was assessed with the Schedule of Attitudes Towards Hastened Death (SAHD-Mx). Results A total of 19 participants (12 in the ketamine group, 7 in the placebo group) and 12 participants (8 in the ketamine group, 4 in the placebo group) were included in the intention-to-treat (ITT) and per-protocol (PP) populations, respectively. Results showed a decrease in BEDS-Mx and SAHD-Mx scores among ITT patients treated with ketamine vs. placebo (from 13.6 to 4.6 vs. 13.3 to 11.7 [p =0.0018]; from 4.0 to 0.5 vs. 3.7 to 3.6 [p =0.0093] across visit 1–4) and in the PP population (13.9 at baseline to 4.4 by the fourth study visit vs. from 13.8 to 12.7 [p =0.0001]; 3.7 at baseline to 0.2 by the fourth study visit vs. from 3.0 to 4.2 by the final visit [p =0.00001]). There were no serious adverse events reported. Significance of results Ketamine is a safe and effective rapid-onset intervention that improves depressive symptoms and decreases WTHD in advanced cancer.

title: Enhanced recovery after surgery in colorectal surgery: Do average benefits mask heterogeneous effects in patients underrepresented in trials?
abstract: For elective colorectal surgery, enhanced recovery protocols are now standard practice, with convincing trial evidence showing fewer complications and shorter stays. What we know far less about is whether that same evidence reliably applies to the patients who were routinely excluded from those trials, older frail adults, those with severe obesity, and people carrying multiple chronic conditions. Three observations from the available data give reason for caution. First, baseline physiological vulnerability predicts complications irrespective of protocol fidelity, a finding that suggests the benefit of compliance is not uniform across patient groups. Second, patients least likely to meet trial eligibility complete fewer elements of the protocol; whether such shortfalls reflect sound clinical judgement or inadvertent undertreatment has not been established. Third, socioeconomic disadvantage and ethnic minority background are linked to wider adherence gaps and poorer outcomes, even where institutional compliance appears high. These signals converge on a single gap in measurement. Existing audit systems document whether a protocol step was carried out, but not why it was omitted. A framework that fails to account for why protocol steps are omitted cannot distinguish clinical adaptation from neglect. Building that distinction into perioperative audit may matter as much for the patients at the margins of evidence as achieving higher compliance scores does for the average patient.

title: Capturing patient preferences to optimize perioperative decision-making in hip and knee arthroplasty: a systematic review of discrete choice experiment studies
abstract: Background Hip and knee arthroplasty effectively treats advanced osteoarthritis, while perioperative decision-making is complex. Clarifying patient preferences helps optimize care, satisfaction and outcomes. This study systematically synthesized evidence on the general public and THA/TKA recipients/candidates’ preferences for perioperative healthcare services. Methods Six databases were searched from inception to December 26, 2025. Two researchers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed methodological quality and risk of bias using the ISPOR checklist and the ROBVALU tool, respectively. Attributes were classified using the healthcare access framework. Frequency, statistical significance, and relative importance were synthesized. Subgroup analyses were performed by perioperative phase, patient status, and country, and preference interactions were examined. Results Of 618 studies, 21 were included (6 countries, 89,407 participants; all high quality on the ISPOR checklist with a low overall risk of bias on the ROBVALU assessment). A total of 142 attributes were classified into five dimensions: availability (63.4%), accommodation (14.8%), acceptability (14.1%), accessibility (4.2%), affordability (3.5%). Availability ranked first in 81.8% of studies, with therapeutic efficacy and treatment safety as top subcategories. Acceptability ranked first in 9.1%. Subgroup analyses revealed: acceptability dominated preoperatively, availability postoperatively; the general public prioritized acceptability, whereas THA/TKA candidates/recipients valued availability more. Except Canada (preferring acceptability), all other countries prioritized availability. Heterogeneity existed by education, age, gender, race, employment, pain, physical function, and diagnosis. Conclusion Availability (especially therapeutic efficacy and treatment safety) is the most valued attribute for perioperative care in THA/TKA, with preferences varying by phase, patient subgroup, country, and individual characteristics. Healthcare administrators and policymakers should prioritize patient preferences and integrate key valued attributes into clinical practice and health policies to optimize THA/TKA perioperative care quality and patient experiences. Systematic review registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261286593. This study was registered on PROSPERO (registration No.: CRD420261286593).

title: The Effect of Transversus Abdominis Plane Block And Conventional Analgesia on Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting and Analgesia Quality in Patients Undergoing Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy, and its Relationship with Complete Blood Count Parameters
abstract: Objective: Transversus abdominis plane (TAP) block is widely utilized for postoperative analgesia following laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Particularly with the posterior approach, local anesthetic dispersion within the fascial plane is reported to be superior, thereby providing effective analgesia. This study aimed to investigate the quality of analgesia and postoperative nausea and vomiting scores between patients undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy who received bilateral posterior TAP block and those who did not.Materials and Methods: In this retrospective study, medical records of 133 patients who underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy between May 2024 and October 2024 were analyzed. Patients were categorized into three groups: two groups that received TAP blocks and one group that received conventional analgesia. Demographic data, pain scores, nausea and vomiting scores, antiemetic administration, and analgesic consumption were evaluated.Results: The study demonstrated that nausea and vomiting scores at the 8th and 12th postoperative hours were significantly higher in the Analgesic group compared to the TAP-2 group (p = 0.002 and p = 0.045). Furthermore, Visual Analog Scale (VAS) scores at 8, 12, and 24 hours were significantly lower in the TAP-2 group compared to the Analgesic group (p < 0.05). The 24-hour analgesic requirement was found to be significantly higher in the Analgesic group compared to the TAP-1 and TAP-2 block groups (p = 0.036).Conclusion: This study has shown that a bilateral posterior TAP block improves postoperative pain relief in patients undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy and that this may be associated with the prevention of postoperative nausea and vomiting.

title: Association Between Non‐Selective β‐Blocker Administration and Overall Survival Among Patients With Intermediate‐Stage Hepatocellular Carcinoma and Clinically Evident Portal Hypertension Following Transarterial Chemoembolization: A Multicenter Retrospective Cohort Study (CHANCE‐CHESS2301)
abstract: Aim Portal hypertension (PH) commonly coexists with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and may influence treatment outcomes, yet the role of PH‐directed therapy in intermediate‐stage HCC remains unclear. This study aims to assess the impact of non‐selective beta‐blockers (NSBBs) on preventing decompensation and enhancing survival in intermediate‐stage HCC patients with clinically evident portal hypertension (CEPH). Methods This multicenter, retrospective, observational cohort study comprised 1614 consecutive HCC patients who underwent transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) between June 2006 and December 2019. CEPH was defined by the presence of any of the following factors: (1) esophageal/gastric varices on endoscopy/computed tomography, (2) diuretic‐treated ascites, (3) splenomegaly with platelet count < 100,000/mm 3. Patients with CEPH were further classified according to whether they received non‐selective beta‐blockers (NSBBs). The primary outcome was overall survival (OS). PH‐related adverse events (AEs) were recorded for CEPH patients. Propensity scores were estimated using logistic regression for propensity score matching, and survival outcomes were analyzed using Kaplan‐Meier analysis and Cox proportional hazards regression. Results Among 1614 patients, 504 (31.2%) had CEPH, and 36 received NSBBs. After 1:1 matching, 418 patients were included in CEPH and non‐CEPH groups. CEPH group exhibited significantly lower median OS compared to non‐CEPH group (23.4 vs. 32.7 months, p = 0.004; adjusted hazard ratio [HR] 1.33, p = 0.003). Prognosis was notably worse in patients with ≥ 2 CEPH factors than in those with 0 or 1 factor (p < 0.001). Within CEPH group, 32 NSBB‐treated and 104 non‐NSBB‐treated patients remained post 1:4 matching. NSBB use correlated significantly with positive outcomes (median OS, 39.2 vs. 21.6 months; p = 0.030; adjusted HR 0.53, p = 0.023). The NSBB group experienced fewer PH‐related complications than the non‐NSBB group (31.2% vs. 43.3%). Conclusion The presence of CEPH significantly correlates with poor prognosis in intermediate‐stage HCC. In TACE‐treated patients with CEPH, NSBB use is associated with longer OS and a lower incidence of PH‐related complications. The association with NSBB use warrants prospective confirmation. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials. gov identifier: NCT05703750

title: Comparative Outcomes of Laparoscopic Surgery for Superior Mesenteric Artery Syndrome: A Retrospective Cohort Study
abstract: AIM: Superior mesenteric artery syndrome (SMAS) is a rare but potentially debilitating cause of proximal intestinal obstruction resulting from vascular compression of the third portion of the duodenum. While surgical intervention is indicated in patients unresponsive to conservative therapy, comparative evidence between laparoscopic and open approaches remains limited. This study aimed to evaluate perioperative and long-term outcomes of laparoscopic versus open duodenojejunostomy (DJ) in patients with SMAS. METHODS: In this retrospective cohort study, 13 consecutive patients diagnosed with SMAS and treated surgically at Dicle University Hospital, a tertiary referral center in Diyarbakır, Turkey between January 2017 and September 2024 were analyzed. Patients were stratified into laparoscopic and open surgery groups. Demographic characteristics, operative variables, postoperative outcomes, and follow-up data including body mass index (BMI) changes and symptom resolution were compared between the groups. RESULTS: A total of 13 patients (9 females, 4 males) with a median age of 26 years (range: 17–59) were included. Six patients underwent laparoscopic duodenojejunostomy, while seven underwent open procedures. Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics were generally comparable between the groups, with the exception of symptom onset time, which was significantly longer in the laparoscopic group (44.3 ± 16.5 vs. 22.0 ± 16.1 months, p = 0.032). Operative time did not differ significantly between laparoscopic and open surgery (103.3 ± 68.8 vs. 95.0 ± 52.0 minutes, respectively; p > 0.05). The laparoscopic group demonstrated a significantly shorter hospital stay (median: 5.5 [3–6] days vs. 7 [6–9] days; p = 0.008). During follow-up, mean BMI values increased in both groups, with no statistically significant between-group differences at the assessed time points. Postoperative symptoms persisted in one patient in the open surgery group and none in the laparoscopic group (p = 1.000). Postoperative symptom resolution was achieved in 12 of 13 patients (92.3%), and no symptom recurrence was observed during follow-up. CONCLUSIONS: In this small retrospective cohort, laparoscopic duodenojejunostomy was feasible and associated with a shorter hospital stay compared with open surgery. Both approaches resulted in symptom improvement and BMI gain during follow-up. Larger prospective studies are required to clarify comparative long-term effectiveness and establish optimal surgical selection criteria.

title: Robotic surgery in gastrointestinal emergency settings: A systematic review
abstract: BACKGROUND Robotic-assisted surgery has become an established component of elective minimally invasive surgery, yet its role in emergency gastrointestinal surgery remains uncertain. Emergency procedures pose unique challenges, including time-critical decision-making, complex anatomy, and limited opportunities for extensive preoperative planning. AIM To evaluate the current evidence regarding the feasibility, safety, and clinical outcomes of robotic surgery in the emergency gastrointestinal setting. METHODS A systematic literature search of PubMed, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library was performed for studies published through June 15, 2026, following PRISMA guidelines. Eligible studies evaluated robotic-assisted emergency gastrointestinal procedures in adult patients and reported perioperative or clinical outcomes. Study selection, data extraction, and quality assessment were independently performed by two reviewers using validated appraisal tools. Owing to substantial methodological heterogeneity, a descriptive synthesis with pooled weighted means was conducted. RESULTS Thirty-two studies met the inclusion criteria, comprising predominantly retrospective cohort studies with additional case series and case reports. Acute cholecystitis represented the most extensively investigated indication (13242 patients), followed by acute appendicitis (475 patients), emergency colorectal surgery (326 patients), abdominal wall hernias (138 patients), perforated peptic ulcer (25 patients), abdominal trauma, and other rare emergency conditions. Across selected patients, robotic surgery demonstrated high technical feasibility, low conversion rates, acceptable operative times, and favorable postoperative recovery. The largest evidence base concerned acute cholecystitis (13242 patients). Among the subset of studies reporting conversion outcomes, conversion to open surgery occurred in 5 of 792 patients (0.6%). However, evidence for other emergency indications remained limited by small sample sizes, retrospective study designs, heterogeneous patient selection, and inconsistent outcome reporting. High acquisition costs, limited platform availability, prolonged setup times, and the need for specialized surgical teams remain important barriers to widespread implementation. CONCLUSION Robotic surgery is safe and feasible in carefully selected, hemodynamically stable patients when performed in high-volume centres. However, it does not currently represent a paradigm shift in emergency general surgery compared to standard laparoscopy, primarily due to logistical constraints, prolonged operative times, and higher costs. High-quality prospective multicenter studies and randomized trials are required to define appropriate indications, evaluate cost-effectiveness, and establish the role of robotic technology within modern emergency surgical practice.

title: Suspected Testicular Malignancy Under the Two-Week-Wait Pathway: A Four-Year Retrospective Audit of 281 Primary Care Referrals
abstract: Background: The two-week-wait (2WW) pathway aims to shorten the time to diagnosis for suspected testicular cancer. Because testicular cancer is rare and most scrotal pathology is benign, the pathway's diagnostic yield in unselected primary care referrals is uncertain, and the optimal entry test remains debated. Methods: We conducted a retrospective review of 281 general practice referrals to the testicular 2WW pathway between January 2021 and December 2024. We used patient records and WebICE to collect data on age, tumour marker testing, imaging, treatment, and histology. Cancer yield was calculated as histology-confirmed malignancies divided by total referrals. Results: The mean age was 55.8 years; 93 (33.1%) patients were aged under 45 and 188 (66.9%) were aged 45 or older. Tumour markers were recorded for 130 (46.3%) patients. Histology-confirmed malignancy was reported in 21 (7.5% of referrals) patients. Overall, 28 patients underwent orchidectomy: histology showed 21 malignancies, one non-malignant case associated with cryptorchidism, and six benign findings. Annual referral numbers were 82 in 2021, 72 in 2022, 47 in 2023, and 80 in 2024; the reported annual malignancy yields ranged from 6.3% to 9.8%. Conclusion: Most referrals did not result in a histology-confirmed malignancy, and the recorded overall cancer yield was 7.5%. The findings support reviewing how ultrasound is used before referral, particularly for older patients. Any change must still support timely cancer diagnosis and safe referrals.

title: Rapid diagnostics of actionable mutations in acute myeloid leukemia using amplicon nanopore sequencing
abstract: Rapid genetic characterization of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is essential for risk stratification and treatment selection. We developed and clinically implemented a targeted Oxford Nanopore Technologies long-read sequencing assay for simultaneous analysis of NPM1, FLT3, IDH1, IDH2, and TP53. In 36 patients, the assay detected 63/64 previously identified variants (98.4% sensitivity), including FLT3-ITDs. All TP53 variants in independent cohorts were detected and phased, enabling assessment of allelic status. Prospective validation in a clinical setting showed 100% sensitivity and specificity, with a mean turnaround time of ~ 32 hours, supporting streamlined AML diagnostics and patient management.

title: ICG fluorescence-guided laparoscopic Kasai portoenterostomy for biliary atresia: a single-centre observational study
abstract: Objective The aim of this study was to compare perioperative outcomes between indocyanine green (ICG) fluorescence-guided and conventional laparoscopic Kasai portoenterostomy for biliary atresia, in order to evaluate the safety and early recovery benefits of fluorescence navigation and provide preliminary evidence for its clinical application. Methods This observational study included 9 infants with type III biliary atresia who underwent laparoscopic Kasai portoenterostomy at the Second Hospital of Hebei Medical University between January 2023 and March 2025. Patients were divided into ICG fluorescence navigation and conventional laparoscopic groups. Clinical characteristics, surgical outcomes, postoperative recovery, and laboratory parameters were compared using SPSS 26.0. Results The baseline characteristics were comparable between the groups. All operations were completed laparoscopically. The operative time and intraoperative blood loss did not significantly differ. Compared with the control group, the fluorescence group presented a significantly shorter nasogastric tube duration (P < 0.05) and abdominal drainage duration (P < 0.05). The white blood cell count and total bilirubin level were significantly lower on postoperative day 1 (P < 0.05), and the haemoglobin level was significantly greater on postoperative day 7 (P < 0.05) in the fluorescence group. No significant differences were observed in the time to first flatus, resumption of oral intake, hospital stay, jaundice clearance rate, or cholangitis incidence. Conclusion ICG fluorescence-guided laparoscopic Kasai portoenterostomy appeared safe and feasible for type III biliary atresia in this pilot study. Shorter postoperative nasogastric and abdominal drainage tube durations, lower early postoperative white blood cell counts, and an initial decline in total bilirubin were observed in the fluorescence group; however, given the small, non-randomized sample, these exploratory findings do not establish a direct benefit of ICG guidance on postoperative recovery. Preliminary 1-year follow-up showed comparable native liver survival between groups, although the sample size was too small for meaningful comparison. Given the single-centre, non-randomized design and very small sample size, these findings are exploratory and require confirmation through larger, multicentre prospective studies.

title: Case Report: Heterogeneous clinical manifestations of severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome with contrasting clinical courses
abstract: Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) often presents with fever and cytopenia in patients without a recognised tick bite. We describe two patients with contrasting clinical courses. Case 1, a 73-year-old male farmer, presented with abdominal pain, fever and cytopenia; his marrow aspirate was markedly hypocellular (grade IV), ferritin was 806.66 ng/mL, and SFTSV RNA was confirmed by RT-PCR on illness day 25, three days after discharge. He recovered with supportive care. Case 2, a 45-year-old woman, developed fever three days after an insect bite, followed by profound neutropenia (ANC nadir 0.09 × 10 9 /L), thrombocytopenia (nadir 24 × 10 9 /L), ferritin >30,000 ng/mL, hypoxaemic respiratory failure and Streptococcus mitis bacteraemia; mNGS detected 74 SFTSV-specific reads, supporting a diagnosis of probable SFTS. She received mask oxygen for two days, was discharged on illness day 7 and died seven days later. The cytokine panel in Case 2 showed elevated IFN-α and IL-10. Both patients fulfilled three of the eight HLH-2004 criteria. SFTS should be considered in endemic-season fever with unexplained cytopenia, and assessed by diagnostic certainty, inflammatory burden and clinical outcome.

title: Prognostic value of the EtCO2-derived alveolar dead-space fraction in a heterogeneous mechanically ventilated intensive care unit cohort: a prospective observational study
abstract: Background The alveolar dead-space fraction derived from end-tidal CO 2 (AVDSF = (PaCO 2 − EtCO 2)/PaCO 2) is a bedside estimate of ventilatory efficiency and has been associated with adverse outcomes in critically ill patients. Its relationship with mortality is uncertain because extrapulmonary disturbances affect EtCO 2. We investigated the association between AVDSF and intensive care unit (ICU) mortality in mechanically ventilated patients after excluding major conditions affecting EtCO 2 measurements. Methods This prospective single-center observational study enrolled mechanically ventilated adult ICU patients between November 2024 and April 2025. Patients with conditions potentially affecting EtCO 2 -derived measurements were excluded. Respiratory and gas exchange variables were recorded during the first three days of ventilation; first-day AVDSF and the mean of all available measurements during the first three calendar days of mechanical ventilation (3-day mean) were analyzed. Associations with ICU mortality were estimated by Firth penalized logistic regression, unadjusted and adjusted for APACHE II. Results Of 329 ICU admissions, 126 patients required invasive mechanical ventilation and 68 were analyzed; ICU mortality was 47.1% (n = 32). Mortality was 59.1% with 3-day mean AVDSF >0.20 and 41.3% with AVDSF ≤0.20 (p = 0.169). The unadjusted OR for ICU mortality was 1.36 per 0.10 increase in 3-day mean AVDSF (95% CI, 0.91–2.09) and 2.00 for AVDSF >0.20 (0.73–5.65); after adjustment for APACHE II, the ORs were 1.13 (0.72–1.78) and 1.28 (0.42–3.86). The AUC was 0.59 (0.45–0.73) for the 3-day mean and 0.55 (0.41–0.69) for day-1 AVDSF. Patients with AVDSF >0.20 had lower VCO 2, VO 2, PaO 2 and PaO 2 /FiO 2 and higher PaCO 2, plateau pressure, peak pressure, driving pressure, and respiratory system elastance (all p < 0.05), whereas PEEP and minute ventilation were similar. Conclusion In this small, selected cohort of mechanically ventilated patients, a statistically clear association between EtCO 2 -derived AVDSF and ICU mortality was not demonstrated after adjustment for illness severity; given the limited precision, a clinically relevant association cannot be excluded. AVDSF was associated with impaired oxygenation and less favorable respiratory mechanics in exploratory analyses.

title: Paradigm shift in the management of complex paediatric tracheal surgery: evolution of a national critical airway team at a large tertiary referral centre
abstract: Background Complex tracheal disease in children is rare and heterogeneous, and its surgical management is technically demanding. Although tracheal surgery was the last to develop in the field of cardiothoracic surgery, it has evolved tremendously to produce impressive results since its start in the 1950s. In the UK, care for these patients has been centralised at a single national referral centre. We describe the development of this service and its multidisciplinary tracheal team (MDTT) between 1995 and 2022, including changes in the case mix, operative practice and perioperative care. We also report selected clinical outcomes following slide tracheoplasty across three eras of service development. Methods We conducted a retrospective descriptive review of referral activity and surgical management of all children referred to the tracheal service at Great Ormond Street Hospital, London, between January 1995 and July 2022, supplemented by a historic account of service development. Outcomes after slide tracheoplasty were described across three eras: 1995-1999 (before a dedicated MDTT), 2000-2010 (formation of the MDTT and designation as the national centre), and 2011-2022 (expansion of the team, with routine interventional radiology and hybrid approaches). Data are presented descriptively. Results A total of 1,272 children were referred to our service covering a wide spectrum of tracheal diseases. Operative management included slide tracheoplasty (n = 212), patch tracheoplasty (n = 47) due to trauma (n = 3) or tumours (n = 21), resection with end-to-end anastomosis (n = 7), and aortopexy (n = 121) or tracheopexy (n = 29) for tracheomalacia. Comparing 1995-1999, 2000-2010 and 2011-2022, in-hospital mortality was 16.7% vs 7.5% vs 6.3%, respectively. Service development included MDTT case review, intraoperative airway assessment and interventional management of postoperative obstruction. Since attaining the status of a national centre for tracheal diseases and formation of MDTT in 2000, a comprehensive treatment algorithm has been established. Conclusion Over almost three decades, paediatric tracheal surgery at our centre grew from a small number of homograft reconstructions into a centralised multidisciplinary national service managing increasingly complex disease. Standardised referral pattern and team dynamics amidst a difficult clinical environment with extreme complexity helped achieve persistent results over years. The practical lessons of building such a service may inform other centres developing paediatric airway programmes.

title: Selective preoperative assessment before early laparoscopic cholecystectomy: A narrative review
abstract: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy is recommended for symptomatic gallstone disease, acute cholecystitis and mild gallstone pancreatitis because it reduces recurrent biliary events and avoidable readmission. Formal preoperative assessment remains essential when comorbidity, frailty, medication complexity or anaesthetic concerns require investigation or optimization. Whether every low-risk patient needs a separate clinic-based appointment before early surgery is less certain. This narrative evaluates the evidence relevant to selective preoperative assessment, drawing on guidelines, routine-testing studies, perioperative risk literature and an illustrative five-year United Kingdom Hot Gallbladder Pathway service evaluation involving 511 patients. Current guidance supports individualized investigation but does not define criteria for omitting preassessment. Indirect evidence suggests that structured screening, review of recent clinical information and same-day anaesthetic confirmation may provide a feasible pathway for carefully selected American Society of Anesthesiologists I-II patients without red flags. The United Kingdom service evaluation reported no identified anaesthetic-related adverse event and one non-anaesthetic cancellation, but its retrospective single-trust design cannot establish equivalence, rare-event safety or cost-effectiveness. Selective assessment should therefore be regarded as a governed service model rather than an established standard. Prospective multicentre studies should compare cancellation, perioperative complications, unplanned admission, time to surgery, patient experience, resource use and cost-effectiveness.

title: Preventive strategies for post-endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography pancreatitis: A systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: BACKGROUND Post-endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) pancreatitis (PEP) is a common and clinically significant adverse event following ERCP. Although pharmacological and endoscopic prophylactic measures have been widely investigated, the implications of these strategies for perioperative nursing pathways require systematic synthesis. AIM To investigate the effects of preventive strategies on the risk of PEP and summarize the clinical implications for standardized perioperative nursing practice. METHODS Chinese and international databases, including the China National Knowledge Infrastructure, Wanfang, the VIP Database for Chinese Technical Periodicals, the China Biology Medicine disc, the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, PubMed, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library, were searched from January 2016 to February 2026. Randomized controlled trials comparing preventive interventions with conventional care, placebo, blank control, or routine treatment in adult patients undergoing therapeutic ERCP and reporting PEP events were considered eligible. Risk ratios with 95% confidence intervals were pooled using Review Manager 5.4.1. Heterogeneity was evaluated using the χ 2 test and the I 2 statistic. RESULTS Fourteen randomized controlled trials involving 4788 participants were included. PEP occurred in 93 of 2374 patients in the intervention groups and 249 of 2414 patients in the control groups. Preventive strategies significantly reduced the risk of PEP compared with control conditions (risk ratio = 0.38, 95% confidence interval: 0.30-0.48, P < 0.00001), with no statistically significant heterogeneity (I 2 = 0%, P = 0.77). Most included interventions involved pharmacological prophylaxis, primarily non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug-based regimens, or prophylactic pancreatic duct stenting. Risk-of-bias assessment revealed common limitations related to blinding, allocation concealment, and reporting of outcome assessment procedures. CONCLUSION Current evidence supports the implementation of structured perioperative nursing pathways for PEP prevention through risk screening, timely care coordination, close monitoring, and patient education.

title: Correction: Multimodal neuroimmune diagnostic profiling for pediatric lower urinary tract dysfunction associated with occult sacral nerve abnormalities
abstract: Pediatric lower urinary tract dysfunction (LUTD) is a clinically significant continuum of storage and voiding urinary dysfunction that can lead to urinary incontinence, frequent urinary tract infection, residual urine, bladder remodeling, psychosocial stress, and possible upper urinary tract trauma in cases of high-pressure bladder dysfunction. Pediatric nomenclature is crucial because clinical terminology changes with age, continence maturation, bowel processes, and neurodevelopment; therefore, adult nomenclature does not apply directly to children [1,2].Neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction (NLUTD) has been historically accepted concerning children with evident spinal dysraphism, myelomeningocele, or spinal injury, or known neurological disease; however, a challenging diagnostic group comprises children with suspected occult sacral nerve abnormalities but a persistent LUTD despite the absence of overt external spinal abnormality or initial definite radiographic evidence [3,4].In clinical practice, these children can first be defined as having functional non-neurogenic voiding dysfunction because the urgency, frequency, continuity of the urinary stream, daytime wetting, straining, and post-void urine residue largely overlap between neurogenic and nonneurogenic phenotypes. Traditional assessment is based on history, voiding diary, physical examination, urinalysis, renal-bladder ultrasound, uroflowmetry, and the chosen urodynamic evaluation. These approaches are useful, though they often characterize the final bladder phenotype rather than the upstream neural pathway. Urodynamic studies remain a significant method for assessing pediatric LUTD. However, interpretation has been reported to require childspecific methods, artifact control, age-adjusted estimates of bladder capacity, and standardized reporting [2]. Imaging urodynamics can describe detrusor compliance, flow patterns, and coordination of sphincter activity, but not specifically sacral neural impairment or immunemediated tissue maintenance (Table S1).High-frequency perineal or rectal ultrasound provides an additional dynamic structural assessment of bladder neck mobility, detrusor morphology, urethral sphincter thickness, pelvic floor behavior, and post-void structural changes. Neuroelectrophysiology, such as pelvic floor electromyography (EMG) and sacral reflex latency, provides functional evidence of neuromuscular coordination and sacral pathway integrity. Nevertheless, none of the modalities is likely to identify any individual among occult sacral neuropathy, severe functional voiding dysfunction, and transient urinary symptoms in any reliable way. This limitation supports a multimodal diagnostic approach that combines anatomic imaging, functional pressure-flow data, electrophysiological findings, and biological signatures (Table S1).The neuroimmune framework is scientifically pertinent, as bladder management is not purely mechanical. The urothelium is a stretch-receptive, immunologically active interface that reacts to stretch, neural factors, infection-related stimuli, and inflammatory mediators.Experimental and translational evidence shows that lower urinary tract function relies on coordinated communication among urothelial cells, afferent nerves, autonomic efferent nerves, hiatal smooth muscle, and immune mediators [5][6][7]. Nowadays, neuroimmune communication is widely accepted as a general biological process in which nervous system activity can influence immune activation and tissue homeostasis [8]. Chronic neural dysregulation in the bladder can promote sustained urothelial stress, disrupted afferent signaling, cytokine release, mast cell or macrophage stimulation, and progressive detrusor remodeling. In neurogenic and non-neurogenic LUTD, overactive bladder, interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome, and bladder sensory disorders, urinary biomarkers have been examined, including interleukin-6 (IL-6), interleukin-8 (IL-8), tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha), nerve growth factor (NGF), and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1). Still, pediatric evidence is limited and heterogeneous [9][10][11][12]. Primary objective: To assess the diagnostic validity of a combined model comprising highfrequency perineal/rectal ultrasound, urodynamic variables, neuroelectrophysiological variables, and urinary inflammatory biomarkers to distinguish occult sacral neuropathy-related LUTD from functional non-neurogenic LUTD and age-matched controls. The main outcome was the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of the integrated model. We used a retrospective pediatric diagnostic-model cohort design (Figure 2). The development dataset included 120 complete records: 45 occult sacral neuropathy-associated LUTD, 45 functional non-neurogenic LUTD, and 30 controls obtained from Shanghai Children's Medical Center Guizhou Hospital. An independent external validation dataset comprised 90 records from two sites at Guizhou Provincial People's Hospital, including 30 children with occult sacral neuropathy-associated LUTD, 30 with functional non-neurogenic LUTD, and 30 controls, which was independent of the development cohort and used the same prespecified eligibility criteria, predictor definitions, and reference-standard adjudication framework. We applied the locked six-predictor model to the external dataset using the development-cohort centering and scaling constants, without refitting coefficients, reselecting predictors, recalibrating, or optimizing thresholds. Predictor definitions were the same across datasets, while site-specific distributions differed, allowing us to evaluate transportability. We collected medical data and records between January 2020 and December 2025. Exclusion criteria were overt congenital spinal dysraphism, spina bifida or myelomeningocele, active urinary tract infection, prior spinal or pelvic surgery, major congenital malformation of the urinary tract, missing locked predictors, or incomplete biomarker records.Multidisciplinary clinical consensus, based on clinical manifestations, spinal or pelvic MRI findings where present, neurological examination, urodynamic interpretation, and longitudinal follow-up, served as the basis for establishing the diagnostic reference standard. We processed the external validation dataset in the same way.We used electronic medical records, structured urology assessment forms, voiding diaries, parent questionnaires, and archived diagnostic reports to derive clinical variables. Imaging variables comprised bladder neck mobility, detrusor morphology, bladder wall or detrusor appearance, urethral sphincter thickness, and other pertinent post-void findings of high-frequency perineal or rectal ultrasound. Urodynamic variables included bladder compliance, detrusor pressure during filling and voiding, maximum flow rate, pressure-flow pattern, residual urine, and detrusor-sphincter dyssynergy or sphincter non-relaxation. Neuroelectrophysiological outcomes were pelvic floor EMG activity and sacral reflex latency. We used standardized data extraction forms to review all available imaging and functional reports and minimize inter-reviewer differences.There is no definite test for occult sacral neuropathy. Two independent reviewers from the Pediatric Department of Shanghai Children's Medical Center, GuiZhou Hospital, adjudicated the reference-standard diagnosis. Reviewers assessed the prespecified clinical, neurological, imaging, urodynamic, and longitudinal criteria without access to the biomarker composite or model probabilities. Disagreements were resolved by consensus. We applied the same adjudication framework to the development and external validation cohorts. The target-condition label followed a prespecified hierarchical composite reference criterion in line with diagnostic-accuracy precepts [16]. Its components were persistent clinical phenotype, standardized neurological findings, spinal or pelvic MRI when clinically available, conventional urodynamic interpretation, and longitudinal clinical course (Table S2). MRI was supportive when imaging was equivocal, and no single urodynamic abnormality was determinative. The biomarker composite and integrated model probability were not included in the reference-standard label, thereby preventing direct incorporation of the model output into its target. We defined the persistent LUTD phenotype based on longitudinal persistence of lower urinary tract symptoms and the prespecified referencestandard criteria rather than on treatment response. The retrospective dataset did not systematically capture detailed prior bladder-directed medication exposure, so we did not incorporate it into phenotype classification.We created variables and verified them against a prespecified data dictionary based on the manuscript framework and published research on pediatric lower urinary tract. Ultrasound variables included bladder-neck movement, detrusor thickness, urethral-sphincter thickness, and post-void structural results. Urodynamic variables included bladder compliance, detrusor pressure, maximum flow rate, residual urine, and outlet discoordination. Pelvic-floor EMG activity and sacral-reflex latency were neuroelectrophysiological variables. Before model analysis, we checked range, coding, completeness, and cross-variable consistency.To address preanalytical variation, we recorded explicit biomarker-handling metadata for each case. As shown in Table S3, the protocol specified urine collection before urodynamic catheterization, centrifugation at 3000 or 5000 x g for 10 minutes, aliquot volumes of 1.0 or 1.5 mL, uninterrupted storage at -80 °C, and no more than two freeze-thaw cycles. Storage duration had a median of 33.5 months (IQR, 18.0-41.3; range, 1-60) in development and 25.5 months (IQR, 15.3-36.0; range, 1-47) in the external dataset. We quantified urinary IL-6, IL-8, TNF-α, NGF, and MCP-1 using commercially available human ELISA kits (Elabscience Biotechnology Inc., Wuhan, Hubei, China) according to the manufacturer's instructions. We analyzed samples in duplicate and determined concentrations from plate-specific standard curves with appropriate assay controls. Urine samples were centrifuged at 3000-5000 × g for 10 min, aliquoted into 1.0 to 1.5 mL volumes, stored continuously at -80°C, and subjected to no more than two freeze-thaw cycles. Laboratory personnel were blinded to diagnostic classification. Biomarker concentrations were normalized to urinary creatinine and expressed as pg/mg creatinine. These parameters were consistent with published urine-biomarker processing studies and pediatric urinary NGF studies [17,18]. Table S3. Urinary biomarker preanalytical and analytical proceduresThe composite-reference-standard diagnosis of occult sacral neuropathy-related LUTD was a binary result. We based the prespecified predictors on six domains: sacral-reflex latency, bladder compliance, biomarker composite score, detrusor thickness, age, and sex (Table S4).We retained continuously measured predictors on their original scale and standardized them using development-cohort means and population standard deviations. We defined the biomarker composite as the average of standardized natural-log IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha, NGF, and MCP-1 concentrations.We built and locked a multivariable logistic model; we validated it internally using 1000 bootstrap repetitions and evaluated performance. We then calculated optimism as bootstrap apparent performance minus bootstrap test performance, and compared it to the original apparent performance. We quantified discrimination using AUC and overall prediction error using a Brier score. We evaluated calibration intercept with a logistic model in which the outcome was regressed on the predicted logit as an offset; we evaluated calibration slope by regressing the logit outcome on the predicted logit using the freely estimated intercept and slope. Reporting We applied the locked equation to the 90-record external-site dataset, using the development-cohort centering and scaling constants and a threshold of 0.50 without modification (Table S5). We did not refit coefficients, recalibrate, select predictors, or optimize thresholds. We evaluated pooled and site-specific AUCs, Brier score, sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values, calibration intercept, and calibration slope. We used stratified nonparametric bootstrap resampling to obtain 95 percent confidence intervals. This analysis evaluated transportability in the independent external dataset.Secondary analyses included group biomarker distributions and correlations between cytokines, ultrasound remodeling, urodynamics, EMG, sacral-reflex latency, and symptom severity. We chose Pearson or Spearman correlation based on distributional considerations. We included age and sex in the locked equation to account for developmental and demographic variability. All locked-model predictors were complete in both the development and validation datasets; therefore, we did not impute data for the primary analysis.We checked and removed identifiers before analysis; compared ranges and units with the data dictionary; corrected logically impossible combinations; and confirmed completeness checks showed all locked predictors had complete data. We compared distributional summaries across the development and external validation cohorts to identify differences in case mix and predictor distributions. Biomarker quality-control checks included standard-curve, duplicate-well, and batch-effect verification.We mitigated potential bias through prespecified predictor definitions, separating model probabilities from label generation, bootstrap validation, and locked external application.Reporting followed STARD and TRIPOD+AI guidance on reference-standard description, model specification, discrimination, calibration, and interpretation [16,19]. We waived informed consent because we used retrospective anonymous records. In accordance with the ethics approval, we analyzed all data anonymously and reported only aggregate data.The development dataset consisted of 120 complete cases: 45 target-condition cases, 45 functional non-neurogenic LUTD comparators, and 30 controls. The external transportability dataset included 90 complete observations from two sites: 30 target-condition cases and 60 noncases (Figure 3). In the development dataset, the target-condition group showed a coherent structuralremodeling profile, with higher detrusor thickness, lower bladder-neck mobility, and higher outletdiscordance markers than the functional-LUTD and control groups. These differences supported the hypothesis that sacral-pathway abnormality can be accompanied by structural and dynamic outlet variability (Figure 4 and Table 1).Target-condition records were characterized by lower bladder compliance, greater detrusor pressure, lower maximum flow, increased post-void residual, prolonged sacral-reflex latency, and more frequent pelvic-floor EMG abnormalities than comparator records. The urinary inflammatory and neurotrophic markers varied stepwise across the targetcondition, functional-LUTD, and control groups. Urinary IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha, NGF, and MCP-1 concentrations were highest in the occult sacral neuropathy-related LUTD group, intermediate in the functional non-neurogenic LUTD group, and lowest in controls, consistent with the proposed neuroimmune phenotype (Table 2). Mann-Whitney U test. Controls are presented for descriptive reference and were not included in the reported pairwise comparisons.The exploratory single-domain classifiers had moderate-to-strong development-cohort discrimination (AUC, 0.78-0.86), and the integrated multimodal classifier had an AUC of 0.94 (Figure 5A-B andAfter controlling for age and sex, the exploratory association model identified prolonged sacral-reflex latency, low bladder compliance, high biomarker composite score, and increased detrusor thickness as independent correlates, which differed conceptually from the locked continuous-predictor diagnostic equation (Table 5). Random-forest feature ranking identified the same domains as the most prominent (Figure 7). Correlation analysis showed that the biomarker composite was positively associated with ICCS symptom score, detrusor pressure, and detrusor thickness, and negatively associated with bladder compliance, indicating that neural, inflammatory, and remodeling signals converge (Table 6, Figure 8). This study characterized a candidate multipolar neuroimmune diagnostic phenotype and evaluated the model using bootstrap internal validation and independent external validation. The locked six-predictor model showed good discrimination after 1,000-repetition bootstrap optimism reduction (AUC, 0.920), with an average calibration intercept near zero and a slope near one. When applied to an independent two-site dataset without refitting, it yielded an AUC of 0.928, a calibration slope of 0.887, and a negative calibration intercept indicating moderate overprediction.These results highlight the need to understand discrimination and calibration together, rather than relying on AUC alone [20,21].This aligns with pediatric continence standards, which posit that lower urinary tract symptomatology should be interpreted using child-specific terminology, developmental context, and conventional urodynamic reporting [1,2,15,[22][23][24]. It also aligns with more recent pediatric neurogenic bladder recommendations, which base risk stratification on functional bladder behavior, upper-tract protection, and close monitoring rather than symptoms alone [3]. The innovation of the current framework is that it adds an immunologically informed component to the existing structural and functional assessment pathway.The key biological message is the association between dysfunction of occult sacral pathways and urinary immune activation. Micturition requires coordinated afferent stimulation, autonomic discharge, and relaxation of the detrusor and sphincter muscles [5,6,13]. The urothelium is not a passive barrier; rather, it is an active interface of the senses and the immunological response that can respond to stretch, neural stimuli, infection-associated stimuli, and inflammatory mediators [7]. Thus, the self-reinforcing pathway of chronic sacral dysregulation can plausibly bring about urothelial stress, the release of local cytokines and neurotrophins, afferent sensitization, and a progressively remodeled detrusor.In the latter framework, high IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha, NGF, and MCP-1 are not considered disease-specific markers on their own. Cytokine elevations can also result from infection, irritation, overdistension, or other inflammatory conditions. They are valuable because they are correlated with delayed sacral reflex latency, abnormal pelvic floor EMG, low bladder compliance, high detrusor pressure, and detrusor thickening. This convergence between findings supports a neuroimmune phenotype. Recent neuroimmune biology also suggests that neuroimmune signaling can link nervous system activity and immune signaling, forming clinical feedback loops that regulate one another [8].The hypothesis for future clinical testing is that persistent urgency, interrupted stream, straining, escalated residual urine, or frequent urinary symptoms might be examined when structural, urodynamic, neuroelectrophysiological, and inflammatory results converge on three or four points. Prospective diagnostic-impact studies in pediatric populations are needed to address those questions.The combined model is still experimental. title: Impact of a respiratory therapy-driven early rehabilitation nursing protocol on clinical outcomes in neonates with hyperbilirubinemia, pneumonia, or systemic infection
abstract: Aim To evaluate the impact of a respiratory therapy-driven early rehabilitation nursing protocol on clinical outcomes in neonates with hyperbilirubinemia, pneumonia, or systemic infection in a primary-level hospital without a Pediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU). The protocol integrates airway clearance, positioning optimization, progressive passive movement, respiratory muscle stimulation, and kangaroo mother care into a single nurse-delivered intervention, a combination not previously evaluated in this population or setting. Methods This single-center retrospective cohort study included 106 neonates admitted between October 2020 and October 2025. Because the nursing protocol was implemented at a fixed calendar time point, group classification was entirely determined by admission period: 52 neonates admitted between October 2020 and September 2022 (pre-implementation period) were classified into the conventional group, and 54 neonates admitted between October 2022 and October 2025 (post-implementation period) were classified into the observation group. This design feature renders the intervention completely confounded with calendar period, a limitation addressed explicitly in the Discussion. Outcomes included length of hospital stay, duration of respiratory support, feeding intolerance, weight gain rate, Neonatal Behavioral Neurological Assessment (NBNA) score, and adverse events. Results Compared with the conventional group, the observation group had significantly shorter hospital stay (11.24 ± 3.92 vs. 13.73 ± 4.95 days, P =0.005), total oxygen therapy duration (4.44 ± 2.83 vs. 7.13 ± 3.69 days, P < 0.001), and time to de-escalation of respiratory support (2.19 ± 1.86 vs. 3.58 ± 3.18 days, P = 0.007). The observation group also showed lower incidence of feeding intolerance (18.5% vs. 38.5%, P = 0.023), higher weight gain rate (15.08 ± 3.21 vs. 11.28 ± 2.70 g/kg/day, P < 0.001), and higher NBNA scores (37.87 ± 1.77 vs. 35.23 ± 2.31, P < 0.001). No significant differences in adverse events were observed between groups. Conclusion In this retrospective cohort, the respiratory therapy-driven early rehabilitation nursing protocol was associated with improved clinical outcomes in neonates with hyperbilirubinemia, pneumonia, or systemic infection, without a statistically significant increase in adverse events, although the sample size (n = 106) and the small number of events (3 vs. 2) provided limited power to detect differences in rare adverse events. However, because the intervention was completely confounded with calendar period, these findings should be interpreted as associative rather than causal. The protocol appears feasible in primary-level neonatal departments without a PICU and warrants further evaluation; prospective multicenter studies with concurrent control groups are needed before widespread clinical promotion and application.

title: A randomized controlled trial comparing the efficacy of cipepofol versus propofol for sedation on choking response in gastroscopy
abstract: Background Cipepofol (HSK3486), a novel γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA A) receptor agonist, recently achieved US FDA approval. While its general sedative efficacy is established, its specific effect on suppressing mechanical reflex responses during gastroscopy remains unclear. This randomized trial investigated the effects of cipepofol in inhibiting the insertion-induced choking response, and its impact on hemodynamics and respiratory safety. Methods This single-blinded, parallel-group trial randomized 200 patients (1:1) to receive cipepofol (0.4 mg/kg) or propofol (2.0 mg/kg) for gastroscopy sedation, co-administered with sufentanil. Propofol (1.0 mg/kg) served as the rescue medication. The primary endpoint was the incidence of choking response upon gastroscope insertion, defined as gagging or movement requiring procedural interruption. Safety assessments included hemodynamics, hypoxemia, and adverse events monitored for 48 h. Results The incidence of choking response was significantly lower in the cipepofol group (22.0%) compared to the propofol group (36.0%) (P < 0.05). Both groups maintained comparable clinical depths of sedation during insertion (MOAA/S score ≤1). When choking occurred, the cipepofol group required less rescue sedative (P < 0.05). Insertion, examination, and alert times were comparable. Cipepofol significantly reduced injection pain (1.0% vs. 59.0%, P < 0.05) and dizziness (P < 0.05). Mean arterial pressure (MAP) upon insertion was higher in the cipepofol group (P < 0.05). Other adverse events did not differ significantly. Conclusion In relatively healthy patients undergoing gastroscopy, cipepofol induced comparable sedation to propofol while demonstrating superior efficacy in inhibiting the choking response. Cipepofol maintained a comparable safety profile with a lower incidence of certain adverse events; however, larger trials are needed to definitively establish its respiratory safety profile in higher-risk populations.
