title: Supporting surgical site infection prevention after caesarean section through self-management kits: A single-centre proof-of-concept quality improvement project
Older adults with frailty and (sub)acute health problems: a descriptive comparison of four different care and cure pathways for aging in place
abstract: Purpose Supporting aging in place among community-dwelling older adults with frailty becomes particularly challenging when (sub)acute health problems arise. This study explored outcomes across care pathways that may reduce the need for crisis-driven emergency department (ED) visits or institutional admissions while maintaining quality of life (QoL) and health perception and reducing caregiver burden (EDIZ). Particular attention was given to Subacute Care Pathway (Subacute Zorgstraat, SaZ), an intermediate care model integrating care and cure. Methods A mixed-methods study was performed in 2023, using data from four different care pathways: SaZ, home visits (HV), outpatient emergency geriatric clinic (OEC), and ED visits. Measures included baseline characteristics, interventions, QoL, health perception, EDIZ and place of residence after 9 months assessed by telephone follow-up and hospital records. Results At the nine-month follow-up, 51 of the 85 enrolled patients were still living at home. Particularly high percentages were seen in SaZ and OEC groups, with few acute admissions to the ED and nursing home during this period. These pathways also had good patient-related outcomes and decreased EDIZ. Post-consultation, SaZ provided both medical and supportive care interventions. Conclusion Care pathways may provide appropriate alternative options to ED care for community‑dwelling older adults with frailty. Particularly, an intermediate care pathway integrating care and cure appears to be promising when the underlying etiology may require both medical and supportive interventions. Larger comparative studies are needed to determine its effectiveness, impact on caregiver burden, and cost-effectiveness.

title: Seizure burden and continuity of care among children with epilepsy during Sudan's armed conflict: A multicenter cross‐sectional study
abstract: OBJECTIVE: We examined how Sudan's armed conflict changed seizure burden and continuity of care for children on established treatment, and whether the disruptions families described were patterned by conflict exposure or household economic position. METHODS: Between 26 April and 23 September 2024, clinicians interviewed caregivers of children aged 2-18 years whose epilepsy had been diagnosed before April 2023, recruited from an online pediatric neurology tele-clinic and two eastern teaching hospitals. Care and seizure burden before the war were compared with those at interview using exact McNemar tests. Outcomes were compared between conflict-affected and relatively spared states using prevalence ratios, with Benjamini-Hochberg control of the false discovery rate, and four prespecified multivariable models. RESULTS: Of 176 interviews, 153 children were analyzed (60.1% male). Follow-up had become irregular for 87 of 152 (57.2%), treatment had been interrupted at least once for 80 of 153 (52.3%), and 66 (43.1%) had lost contact with their physician. The proportion having two or more seizures a month rose from 25.5% to 32.9% (18 deteriorated, 7 improved; exact McNemar p = 0.04). Fifty-six children (36.6%) had a seizure lasting more than 5 min; 34 (60.7%) reached an emergency department immediately and 30 (53.6%) obtained rescue medication. Prolonged seizures (52.1% vs. 28.8%; adjusted prevalence ratio [aPR] 1.74, 95% CI 1.16-2.63) and irregular follow-up (72.3% vs. 51.0%; aPR 1.45, 95% CI 1.11-1.88) were more frequent in conflict-affected states, but neither unadjusted difference remained significant after correction for multiple comparisons (smallest q = 0.12). Interruption of therapy was determined mainly by household income (lowest two bands, aOR 2.98, 95% CI 1.47-6.04) rather than geography. SIGNIFICANCE: Epilepsy care in Sudan has been disrupted along the whole pathway and in every region studied. Cost, not distance from the front line, was the dominant barrier to uninterrupted treatment. PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: Sudan has been at war since April 2023, and we interviewed the families of 153 children who already had epilepsy when the war began. More than half had missed their regular clinic visits, and more than half had run out of their seizure medicine at least once, most often because the family could not afford it. Children living in the states where fighting was taking place were more likely to have long seizures and to miss follow-up, though these differences were not statistically conclusive. Making seizure medicines free would help these children more than any other single measure.

title: Edukasi Diet 3J dan Aktivitas Fisik sebagai Upaya Pemberdayaan Pasien Diabetes Melitus Tipe 2 pada Kegiatan Prolanis
abstract: Type 2 diabetes management requires active patient participation in dietary regulation and physical activity. This community service activity aimed to support patient empowerment through education on the 3J dietary principles and physical activity during the Indonesian Chronic Disease Management Program (Prolanis). Conducted on December 27, 2025, at a hospital’s internal medicine outpatient clinic in Madiun City, the activity involved 25 patients. A single 25–30-minute session used PowerPoint slides, leaflets, and educator-led movement demonstrations. Topics included food quantity, food type, meal timing, walking, and diabetes exercise, marching in place, light arm movements, and family support. Some patients attended with family members. Evaluation involved educator-led oral questions without pretests, posttests, or individual scoring. According to organizers’ observations, participants responded enthusiastically, and those answering questions provided responses consistent with the educational content. These findings reflect understanding demonstrated during the session but do not establish improvements in knowledge, dietary adherence, physical activity, or glycemic control. The session provided opportunities to clarify self-management information for patients and accompanying families. Educational reinforcement and structured follow-up evaluation are recommended to assess the application of the material in daily life.

title: Translational artificial intelligence in therapeutic-era metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis: The ACTION framework
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) has entered a therapeutic era in which priorities extend beyond detecting steatosis to identifying treatment-actionable fibrosis, rationalising referral and biopsy, standardising trial endpoints and monitoring response. Artificial intelligence (AI) spans electronic health records, non-invasive tests, imaging and digital pathology, but reports often omit the user, threshold and consequence. We conducted a structured narrative review and developed the author-proposed ACTION framework. ACTION comprises attached action, calibration in context, threshold-specific benefit, integration, oversight, and non-discrimination and monitoring. Evidence is uneven. Case-finding and enrichment models can identify uncoded or higher-risk patients, but their prospective effects on testing, referral and outcomes remain unproven. Imaging AI supports reproducible quantification, although signals may add little beyond clinical variables. The human-reviewed AI-based measurement tool for MASH (in regulatory records) is among the most mature applications reviewed, within a narrowly specified clinical-trial context. It is qualified for specified MASH clinical-trial workflows, not for autonomous diagnosis or unrestricted treatment selection. AI becomes clinically meaningful only when a calibrated output is linked to a predefined action, an accountable human user and a measurable patient or trial outcome.

title: Sustainability assessment of heavy-duty trucks, part I: a multi-criteria assessment method for comparing alternative technologies
abstract: Transitioning heavy-duty road freight towards more sustainable solutions is a complex challenge, with multiple competing technologies—ranging from renewable fuels to battery-electric and hydrogen systems—each offering distinct advantages and drawbacks. Existing sustainability assessments often focus narrowly on climate impacts or single technologies, limiting their usefulness for fair and comprehensive comparisons. This study develops a multi-criteria assessment (MCA) method for broad sustainability evaluation of heavy-duty truck technologies, including a soft, indicator-based framework developed through an iterative, literature-based and participatory process involving researchers, vehicle manufacturers, utilities, and public organisations. The framework covers four key areas—technical, economic, environmental, and social performance—operationalised through 16 indicators with transparent five-level ordinal rating scales defined by numerical thresholds, qualitative descriptions, or both. The method accommodates both established and emerging technologies, including fossil and renewable energy carriers, combustion and electric/fuel-cell drivetrains. During the development, indicator definitions were refined to reduce avoidable duplication, while some conceptual overlap remains. Designed for decision support, the method does not prescribe weights or an aggregation rule, allowing these choices to be adapted to the decision context. It expands the scope beyond common metrics by including institutional conditions, socio-technical system services, and supply security alongside more conventional technical, cost, and environmental indicators. The MCA method provides a structured yet flexible way of comparing truck technologies and may help identify cross-dimensional trade-offs and potential risks of problem-shifting to support informed choices for sustainable freight transport. In the companion study done by Smolarczyk et al. (2026), the MCA method is applied to a range of truck technologies, which demonstrates its practical use.

title: Real-world clinical outcomes following magnetic e-Resonance therapy for PTSD: retrospective chart review
abstract: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a prevalent and disabling condition for which first-line treatments are often ineffective. Magnetic e-Resonance Therapy (MeRT) is a recently FDA-cleared personalized form of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) for adults with PTSD that delivers stimulation at a patient’s algorithmically derived alpha frequency (8–13 Hz). This retrospective analysis examined clinical outcomes of patients with PTSD who received MeRT in a real-world setting prior to FDA clearance. Twelve civilian patients received 36 daily sessions. PTSD and depressive symptoms were assessed using the PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5) and the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) respectively. PCL-5 scores decreased from a median baseline of 50.0 (IQR, 43.3-57.0) to 30.5 (IQR, 9.5-36.5). In patients with comorbid moderate-to-severe depressive symptoms (n=9), median PHQ-9 scores decreased from 17.0 (IQR, 13.0-24.0) at baseline to 9.0 (IQR, 8.0-14.0). There were no dropouts or serious adverse events. In this real-world case series, MeRT was feasible, well tolerated, and associated with reductions in PTSD and depressive symptoms. Prospective randomized trials are needed to determine whether MeRT provides additional benefit over non-personalized TMS protocols for PTSD.

title: A Lightweight YOLOv8-Based Diagnostic System for Prostatic Acinar Adenocarcinoma: A Comparative Analysis of Architecture, Performance, and Clinical Applicability
abstract: Background Prostate cancer diagnosis relies heavily on accurate Gleason grading, yet conventional pathology faces challenges in consistency and efficiency. Artificial intelligence offers transformative potential, but existing systems remain either prohibitively expensive or closed-source, limiting accessibility. Methods We developed an open-source, YOLOv8-based diagnostic system and validated it on the Gleason2019 Grand Challenge public dataset (250 prostate tissue microarray cores; 190 malignant, 60 benign). Performance was evaluated against consensus diagnoses from six expert pathologists. Metrics included lesion detection rate, Gleason grading concordance (Cohen's Kappa), binary cancer classification (sensitivity, specificity, and area under the curve (AUC)), and inference speed. Multi-dimensional comparison was conducted with research-oriented systems (Thorough Insights, PathOrchestra) and commercial products (Paige Prostate, Tencent AIMIS). Results The system achieved a lesion detection rate of 98.0%. Gleason grading overall accuracy was 76.0%, with a Cohen's Kappa coefficient of 0.831 (almost perfect agreement). Concordance rates by Gleason score were: 78.3% (Gleason 6), 87.9% (Gleason 7), 70.4% (Gleason 8), 44.0% (Gleason 9), and 58.3% (Gleason 10). Binary cancer classification yielded a sensitivity of 84.7%, specificity of 70.0%, and AUC of 0.816 (95% CI: 0.769-0.864). Average inference time was 5.62 seconds per image on an RTX 4080 GPU. Comparative analysis demonstrated that the system balances clinically acceptable performance with complete local deployment, open-source availability, and low cost. Conclusions The YOLOv8-based diagnostic system demonstrates reliable performance on a public prostate cancer dataset. Its open-source, lightweight, locally deployable architecture offers a highly accessible research prototype as an alternative to commercial and closed research systems, potentially serving primary healthcare settings, research laboratories, and medical education.

title: Impact of perioperative Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy on long-term survival after distal gastrectomy for gastric cancer
abstract: BACKGROUND Persistent Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori ) infection is associated with adverse outcomes after gastrectomy for gastric cancer. AIM To evaluate the association of perioperative H. pylori eradication therapy with longterm survival in patients undergoing distal gastrectomy for gastric cancer. METHODS This retrospective cohort study involved H. pylori -positive patients who underwent distal gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy for gastric adenocarcinoma at our hospital from January 2016 to January 2021. The patients were divided into a perioperative eradication group and a non-eradication group depending on whether they received a 14-day bismuth-containing quadruple regimen. Key measurements included H. pylori status at 6 months, nutritional/inflammatory parameters at 12 months, remnant gastric lesions at 1 year, adjuvant chemotherapy completion, and long-term oncologic outcomes, including 5-year overall survival (OS) and disease-free survival (DFS). RESULTS Among the 271 eligible patients (143 non-eradication and 128 eradication), the eradication success rate was 91.41% in the eradication group. Compared with the non-eradication group, the eradication group was associated with significantly higher 5-year OS (91.41% vs 80.42%, P = 0.010) and 5-year DFS (85.94% vs 72.73%, P = 0.008) and lower rates of metachronous gastric cancer (1.56% vs 7.69%, P = 0.018) and gastric cancer-specific death (6.25% vs 15.38%, P = 0.017). Multivariate Cox regression analysis adjusting for age, sex, pathological tumor-node-metastasis stage, differentiation, and lymphovascular invasion revealed that perioperative eradication remained independently associated with improved OS (hazard ratio = 0.551, P = 0.036) and DFS (hazard ratio = 0.604, P = 0.043). CONCLUSION In this retrospective cohort, perioperative H. pylori eradication therapy was independently associated with improved long-term survival and reduced risk of metachronous gastric cancer in patients who underwent distal gastrectomy for gastric cancer.

title: Clinical application of personalized biodegradable anastomotic stent via preoperative intestinal three-dimensions reconstruction in laparoscopic resection of rectal cancer
abstract: BACKGROUND Anastomotic complications affect postoperative recovery in patients with rectal cancer; therefore, more effective treatment strategies are urgently needed. AIM To analyze the clinical value of personalized biodegradable anastomotic reinforcement stents based on preoperative three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction parameters of the intestinal tract in laparoscopic anterior resection for rectal cancer. METHODS A total of 82 patients with rectal cancer who were admitted to our hospital between March 2023 and May 2025 were enrolled and divided into control and study groups according to the order of surgery. Both groups underwent laparoscopic anterior resection of the rectal cancer. The control group underwent conventional anastomosis, whereas the study group underwent implantation of personalized biodegradable anastomotic reinforcement stents based on the preoperative 3D reconstruction parameters of the intestinal tract. Perioperative indicators, postoperative recovery, anastomosis-related complications, postoperative inflammatory response levels and follow-up outcomes were compared between the two groups. RESULTS The stoma duration was longer in the study group than in the control group (P < 0.05). There were no significant differences in intraoperative blood loss, number of dissected lymph nodes, or conversion rate to open surgery between the two groups (P > 0.05). The time to first bowel sound recovery, time to first flatus, time to first oral intake, and time to first ambulation were shorter in the study group than in the control group (P < 0.05). The total incidence of anastomosis-related complications in the study group was 4.88% (2/41), which was lower than 21.95% (9/41) in the control group, with a significant difference (P < 0.05). The levels of inflammatory indicators at 1 day and 3 days after surgery in the study group were lower than those in the control group (P < 0.05). The Wexner incontinence and low anterior resection syndrome scores at 6 months and 12 months after surgery were significantly lower in the study group than in the control group (P < 0.05). CONCLUSION Implantation of personalized biodegradable anastomotic reinforcement stents based on preoperative 3D reconstruction parameters of the intestinal tract can promote postoperative intestinal function recovery, reduce the risk of anastomosis-related complications and inflammatory stimulation, and simultaneously improve postoperative defecation and anal function in patients undergoing laparoscopic anterior resection of rectal cancer.

title: Real-world use of rituximab in rheumatoid arthritis: a three-year analysis from the RBSMR biologic registry
abstract: Background Rituximab (RTX) is generally used in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) after failure of a first biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drug. The international recommendations in force when this registry was established reserved first-line use of RTX for specific circumstances, including residence in a tuberculosis-endemic region. In Morocco, RTX has frequently been used as the first biologic agent because of its favourable tuberculosis safety profile, lower cost and intermittent dosing. This study describes its real-world use, effectiveness and safety in the Moroccan Society of Rheumatology Biologic Registry (RBSMR). Methodology The RBSMR is a multicentre, retro-prospective registry that enrolled 223 patients with RA receiving biologics and followed them every six months for three years. This post hoc analysis included the 170 patients (76.2%) who received RTX at any time, 164 (96.5%) of them as their first biologic agent. The cohort comprised both incident and prevalent users. Effectiveness outcomes were the DAS28-CRP disease-activity state and the EULAR response. Safety outcomes were incidence rates per 100 patient-years (PY) with exact Poisson 95% confidence intervals (CI). Rates were calculated over the maximum observation time (510 PY), which credits every patient with the full three years; they are therefore minimum estimates. Analyses were descriptive. Denominators are reported for every proportion, and non-responder imputation (NRI) over all 170 patients was the only imputation applied. Results Baseline DAS28-CRP was 5.62 ± 1.03 (n = 134). Over a maximum of 510 PY, 42 infectious episodes occurred in 30 patients (8.2 per 100 PY, 95% CI 5.9–11.1), including 6 serious infections in 6 patients (1.2, 95% CI 0.4–2.6). Forty-four non-infectious adverse events were recorded (8.6, 95% CI 6.3–11.6), including two malignancies. In total, ten serious adverse events occurred in nine patients. Rates calculated over on-treatment exposure (475 PY) in a sensitivity analysis were approximately 7% higher. No active tuberculosis occurred during RTX exposure. Remission or low disease activity rose from 1.5% (2/134) at baseline to 45.2% (57/126) at month 6 and 47.4% (65/137) at month 12; it was lowest at months 24 and 30 (32.7% [34/104] and 29.5% [28/95]) and was 41.9% (39/93) at month 36, when the evaluable population was smallest. A good EULAR response was achieved by 44.5% (49/110) of evaluable patients at month 12 and 37.5% (27/72) at month 36; under NRI these proportions were 28.8% (49/170; 95% CI 22.5–36.0) and 15.9% (27/170; 95% CI 11.2–22.1). Conclusions RTX was used predominantly as a first-line biologic agent with on-demand retreatment. Disease activity decreased markedly by month 6, and no new safety concerns were identified, given the small number of events; the reported incidence rates are minimum estimates. Without a comparator group these findings are descriptive and hypothesis-generating. They document the outcomes of this strategy in a tuberculosis-endemic, resource-constrained setting but do not establish that it is superior or equivalent to internationally recommended treatment sequences. Comparative prospective studies are required.

title: A paradigm shift and emerging challenges in precision oncology for liver cancer: a narrative review
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) represents a significant global health challenge, characterized by high genomic, epigenomic, and metabolic heterogeneity. Conventional systemic therapies, including tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) and immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), often encounter efficacy ceilings due to complex resistance networks within the tumor microenvironment (TME). Thisi review examines the paradigm shift in HCC precision oncology driven by high-resolution multi-omics and artificial intelligence (AI). A structured, purposive literature search was conducted across major databases covering publications from January 2010 to September 2026 to synthesize these advancements. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics have elucidated the heterogeneous features of immune cell exhaustion, stromal reprogramming, and spatial communication networks, identifying specific markers for microvascular invasion (MVI) and early recurrence. Furthermore, exosome-mediated epigenetic regulation and spatial metabolic reprogramming reveal deep-seated mechanisms of tumor immune evasion. Concurrently, AI-driven multimodal data integration, including the deployment of open-source large language models (LLMs) in hepatology cohorts, provides candidate tools for predicting immunotherapy efficacy and supporting clinical decision-making, although prospective clinical validation remains limited. To overcome resistance to conventional therapies, targeting metabolic-epigenetic crosstalk and developing innovative drugs based on synthetic lethality—particularly targeting high-frequency HCC alterations such as CTNNB1, ARID1A and TERT promoter mutations—offer promising alternative strategies. Importantly, because clinically validated HCC-specific evidence remains scarce in several of these emerging areas, mechanistic findings derived from other solid tumors are explicitly identified throughout this review as cross-cancer lessons, and their extrapolation to HCC is flagged as requiring validation in liver-specific studies. To support critical appraisal, this review applies a uniform evidence hierarchy—HCC clinical, HCC preclinical, and cross-cancer—and grades each emerging technology by clinical maturity and translational readiness, explicitly separating established practice from exploratory strategy. Despite challenges in data standardization and translational efficiency, the rapid advancement of liquid biopsy technologies, particularly circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) methylation profiling, is driving HCC management toward real-time, non-invasive, and personalized dynamic monitoring. Synergistic interdisciplinary innovation integrating multi-omics atlases, AI predictive models, and liver-targeted delivery systems will provide more precise therapeutic strategies for refractory solid tumors like HCC.

title: Computational Recycling for Sustainability: A Systematic Review on the Recovery of Valuable Materials and the Reduction of Electronic Waste
abstract: The rapid growth of electronic waste, particularly from computer equipment, represents one of today’s major environmental challenges. This systematic review aims to analyze recent scientific literature on computational recycling, with an emphasis on the recovery of valuable materials and the effective reduction of electronic waste. The reviewed studies cover a range of topics, including emerging technologies such as automated disassembly, electrostatic separation, circular economy models, and life cycle analysis. Findings reveal that the application of innovative methods ‒ such as electric disintegration, plastic component valorization, and rare metal recovery ‒ enhances recycling efficiency and reduces environmental burden. However, challenges remain regarding regulation, standardization, and informal recycling practices. The review concludes that computational recycling is key to advancing toward sustainable electronic waste management and a more circular economy.

title: Acute healthcare utilization among children potentially eligible for pediatric palliative care throughout the disease trajectory: a nationwide population-based cohort study
abstract: Background Pediatric palliative care (PPC) aims to improve the quality of life of children with life-limiting or life-threatening conditions through early integration alongside disease-directed treatment. However, many eligible children remain under-recognized and underserved. We aimed to characterize acute healthcare utilization among children with life-limiting chronic conditions in Israel from diagnosis to death, with emphasis on the final year of life, and to compare utilization across age groups and geographic regions. Methods This retrospective population-based cohort study used electronic medical records from Clalit Health Services, Israel's largest health maintenance organization. Children aged 0–18 years diagnosed with life-limiting or life-threatening chronic conditions between 2000 and 2025 were included. Healthcare utilization throughout follow-up was analyzed. Results The cohort included 83,419 children (59.2% male; mean age at diagnosis 5.9 ± 5.9 years), of whom 3,267 (3.9%) died during follow-up. During the final year of life, 43.5% had ≥ 5 hospitalizations (mean 6.3 ± 7.7), 52.7% were admitted to the intensive care unit, and 16.0% had ≥ 5 emergency department visits. Community specialist consultations and imaging were frequent. In contrast, access to palliative care was minimal: 95.7% received no palliative consultation, while only 0.2% received hospice referral or pain consultation. Healthcare utilization differed significantly by age group and geographic region (both p < 0.001). Conclusions Children with life-limiting conditions experience intensive acute healthcare utilization, particularly near the end of life, despite extremely limited access to pediatric palliative care. These findings highlight a persistent gap and support expansion of pediatric palliative care services.

title: Persistent Lymphadenopathy and Mesenteric Lymphadenitis After Influenza and Ebv Infection in an 8-Year-Old Child: Limits of Interpretation of Laboratory and Genetic Markers
abstract: Purpose: Persistent lymphadenopathy is among the most frequent reasons for referral of children to an immunologist, and the increasing availability of laboratory and genetic panels creates a new problem, namely over-interpretation of the results obtained. This case report aims to examine, using a clinical case, the diagnostic approach to persistent post-infectious lymphadenopathy in a child and to discuss the limits of clinical interpretation of selected laboratory and molecular genetic markers. Methods: A single pediatric case was reviewed in accordance with the CARE case-report reporting guideline. Clinical, ultrasound, immunological, etiological, laboratory, and molecular genetic findings were reassessed against current reference values and clinical practice guidelines. Results: An 8-year-old boy was examined for persistent enlargement of submandibular and cervical lymph nodes (up to 32 mm on ultrasound) and mesenteric lymphadenitis, which developed after influenza and a recurrent febrile episode. Cellular and humoral immunity corresponded to age norms and primary immunodeficiency was excluded. Latent tuberculosis was excluded, and the Epstein-Barr virus load corresponded to the latent stage. The complete blood count showed an age-appropriate differential with no reactive lymphocytes or immature cells and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 2 mm per hour; eosinophils accounted for 5% with a calculated absolute count of approximately 0.40 × 10⁹ per L, that is, without eosinophilia. An isolated increase in eosinophil cationic protein up to 102 ng per mL with a normal total immunoglobulin E and an isolated decrease in parathyroid hormone to 8.74 pg per mL with normocalcaemia were detected. Genotyping results led to diagnoses that require revision. Conclusion: Elevated eosinophil cationic protein with normal immunoglobulin E requires mandatory exclusion of parasitic infestation and eosinophilic disorders. Isolated low parathyroid hormone with normocalcaemia requires exclusion of hypomagnesaemia first. The LCT -13910 CT genotype is not a basis for diagnosing primary hypolactasia, and vitamin D receptor gene polymorphisms cannot serve as a basis for adjusting vitamin D dosage.

title: Conceptual engineering design and experimental validation framework for a Bio-Nano Light Pole toward carbon-negative urban infrastructure
abstract: Rapid urbanization has intensified challenges related to air pollution, increasing atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) concentrations, and rising energy demand, highlighting the need for urban infrastructure that may deliver environmental benefits beyond conventional public utilities. This study presents a conceptual engineering design and experimental validation framework for a Bio-Nano Light Pole, a modular biohybrid system proposed to integrate biological carbon assimilation, oxygen generation, bioelectrochemical energy production, air-pollutant treatment, environmental sensing, and energy-efficient illumination within a single urban platform. The proposed architecture combines photosynthetic and electrogenic microorganisms with conductive and photocatalytic nanomaterials in a vertically integrated, cartridge-based design intended to support biological containment, operational flexibility, and routine maintenance. Conductive nanomaterials are proposed to facilitate electron transfer within microbial fuel cells, photocatalytic nanomaterials are proposed for pollutant-treatment applications, and nano-hydrogel encapsulation is proposed to support microbial stability and biosafety under outdoor conditions. A structured experimental validation framework is proposed to evaluate carbon dioxide uptake, oxygen evolution, bioelectricity generation, pollutant-removal efficiency, environmental sensing, and low-energy illumination under controlled pilot-scale conditions. The study provides a reproducible engineering blueprint and quantitative evaluation framework for prototype development and future pilot-scale investigations. Importantly, carbon-negative performance is treated as a future testable hypothesis rather than an established property. Demonstration of carbon negativity would require experimentally measured carbon uptake and quantified material, energy, operational, maintenance, and end-of-life emissions through transparent life-cycle assessment. Accordingly, the framework does not demonstrate carbon-negative operation.

title: From Anesthesia to Rapid-acting Antidepressant: A Bibliometric Analysis of Global Esketamine Research (2000−2025)
abstract: Objective: Esketamine, initially used as a perioperative anesthetic and analgesic, has recently emerged as a rapid-acting antidepressant for treatment-resistant depression (TRD). This bibliometric study evaluated global research trends, major contributors, and evolving hotspots in esketamine research. Methods: Publications on esketamine from 2000 to 2025 were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection. Bibliometric analyses were conducted using VOSviewer 1.6.20 (Nees Jan van Eck and Ludo Waltman, Leiden University), CiteSpace 6.1.R4 (Drexel University), Bibliometrix 4.1.3 (K-Synth Srl), and SCImago Graphica 1.0.27 (SCImago Lab, University of Granada), and Microsoft Office Excel 2022 (Microsoft) to assess publication trends, countries, institutions, journals, authors, citations, and keyword evolution. Results: A total of 1,136 publications were included. Research output increased markedly after 2019, coinciding with growing interest in psychiatric applications. China had the largest publication volume, whereas the United States showed higher citation counts and stronger international collaboration connectivity within the analyzed dataset. Highly cited studies were concentrated mainly in psychiatry, while anesthesiology was also prominent in the broader co-citation network. Keyword and co-citation analyses revealed a clear shift in research focus from perioperative anesthesia and analgesia to rapid-acting antidepressant effects, particularly in TRD and mood disorders. Conclusion: Esketamine research has expanded rapidly over the study period, with a major transition from anesthetic and analgesic applications toward rapid-acting antidepressant research. The field has become increasingly interdisciplinary, while important questions remain regarding long-term effectiveness, safety, patient stratification, and broader clinical translation. These findings provide an overview of the evolving research landscape and may help inform future clinical and translational research.

title: A Case of Laparoscopic Conversion to Open Surgery for Adult Acute Appendicitis with Abdominal Wall Fibrosis
abstract: Acute appendicitis is a common surgical emergency, which usually requires surgical treatment, but there are a few cases due to their own factors make the operation more difficult. This case report discusses a rare case of acute appendicitis in adults with abdominal cocoon syndrome that required a transition from laparoscopic exploration to open surgery. A 51-year-old male presented to the emergency department with abdominal pain for 24 hours. History, physical examination, laboratory examination and imaging examination were consistent with acute appendicitis. The patient was to undergo laparoscopic appendectomy. However, during laparoscopic exploration, dense intra-abdominal adhesions consistent with abdominal cocoon syndrome were found, limiting access to the surgical field and laparoscopic manipulation. Due to the inability to safely proceed with laparoscopic surgery, the procedure was converted to open appendectomy. The open surgery successfully removed the appendix, and the patient was monitored for postoperative complications. On the tenth day after surgery, the patient was discharged after wound healing and recovery. This case highlights the challenges posed by abdominal cocoon syndrome in laparoscopic appendectomy. In such situations, conversion to open surgery is the correct choice as it can reduce collateral damage and operative time. Further research is needed to better understand the impact of abdominal cocoon syndrome on surgical intervention.

title: The experience of viewing disaster-affected photographs: A philosophical and anthropological examination
Novarecover: An SDN-Based Autonomous Cloud Disaster Recovery Framework
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Cloud-hosted applications require continuous availability, yet an unexpected server or service failure can interrupt access and affect business operations. This paper presents NovaRecover, an SDN-based cloud disaster recovery framework designed around a primary cloud server, a backup server, data backup, health monitoring, and network traffic redirection. The proposed architecture uses Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) to host primary and recovery instances, Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3) as a backup storage option, and a Software-Defined Networking (SDN) controller to manage traffic forwarding through programmable network rules. A Python-based monitoring and recovery component is intended to check service health, identify configured failure conditions, initiate recovery actions, and record events for a web-based monitoring dashboard. The paper describes the architecture, operational workflow, component responsibilities, implementation approach, and an evaluation protocol covering failure detection time, recovery time, service availability, and data recovery point. No measured performance values are asserted in this manuscript; these values must be populated from repeatable experiments on the implemented system before submission. The framework provides a structured basis for evaluating automated recovery in a controlled cloud environment.

title: Supplementary material from "Evolutionary dynamics of agricultural index insurance under meteorological disaster risk"
abstract: Climate disasters can severely impact agricultural incomes and trap farmers in poverty. Agricultural index insurance offers a critical risk mitigation strategy for farmers to enhance resilience against such climatic adversities. Despite the growing attention towards agricultural index insurance, theoretical research on which index insurance is more favoured by farmers and how subsidy mechanisms affect the adoption rate of index insurance is still limited. Here, we construct an evolutionary game theory model that considers three different types of index insurance: individual index insurance (III), collective index insurance (CII) and a hybrid form of both. We study the influence of basis risk, risk aversion and threshold-based subsidy on the degree of insurance adoption among farmers. Our findings suggest that, compared with III and mixed index insurance, CII can more effectively increase the insurance adoption rate among farmers. In addition, implementing threshold-based subsidy can also raise adoption rates, with the effect becoming more pronounced as the subsidy threshold decreases. Furthermore, we find that an increase in basis risk tends to reduce the adoption rate of index insurance; however, when the basis risk is low, this trend is mitigated as the risk aversion increases.

title: Rainfall Analysis and the Volume of Flood Disaster Meted Out in Selected Regions of Tanzania: A Quantitative Ecological Panel Study
journal: Journal of Asia Entrepreneurship and Sustainability
abstract: This study analyze rainfall patterns and flood disaster volume in seven selected regions of Tanzania during 2009–2024. It examined monthly rainfall trends, classified regions according to seasonal rainfall patterns, assessed regional flood-disaster volume, and analyzed the relationship between rainfall variability and flood disaster volume. A quantitative ecological panel design was adopted using 112 region-year observations from Tanzania Meteorological Authority rainfall records and flood-disaster records. Descriptive statistics, trend analysis, coefficient-of-variation measures, hierarchical and K-means clustering, Principal Component Analysis (PCA), fixed-effects panel regression, and supplementary Poisson count models were applied. Dar es Salaam, Dodoma and Morogoro recorded statistically significant upward annual rainfall trends, while the remaining regions showed positive but weaker trends. Three broad seasonal rainfall clusters were identified. The first PCA component explained 79.99% of variation in flood-disaster indicators and supported construction of the Flood Disaster Volume Index (FDVI). Dar es Salaam recorded the highest mean FDVI (0.89), followed by Mtwara (0.48), while Songwe recorded the lowest (-1.08). Maximum monthly rainfall was the strongest predictor of FDVI; the preferred fixed-effects specification recorded a within R² of 0.5911. Rainfall anomaly was also positively and significantly associated with flood-event frequency in the supplementary Poisson models. The study concludes that rainfall intensity, abnormal rainfall conditions and seasonal rainfall structure are important correlates of flood-disaster burden. Region-specific rainfall monitoring, rainfall-triggered early warning, integrated disaster data systems and targeted preparedness are recommended.

title: FLOOD: FIGHTING LOCAL ODDS, OVERCOMING DISASTERS — COMMUNITY HEALTH AND RESILIENCE IN SELECTED FLOOD-PRONE AREAS OF PAMPANGA
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This qualitative descriptive study, titled “FLOOD: Fighting Local Odds, Overcoming Disasters, Community Health and Resilience in Selected Flood-Prone Areas of Pampanga,” was conducted from August 2025 to May 2026. It aims to explore the experiences, health issues, and coping methods of residents in flood-prone areas of Pampanga. Frequent floods in Minalin, Sto. Tomas, and the City of San Fernando disrupt daily life, affect health, and challenge community resilience. Despite existing disaster preparedness programs, there is limited understanding of how residents experience, respond to, and manage these events. Using purposive sampling, 12 participants aged 18 to 59 who have experienced at least two flooding events were recruited. Data were gathered through semi-structured face-to-face interviews, audio recordings with consent, and field notes. Thematic analysis was used to identify patterns and themes related to health challenges, coping strategies, and community resilience. The findings revealed that residents experienced various health concerns, including communicable diseases, skin conditions, and illnesses related to water and sanitation. They also demonstrated preparedness and adaptive coping strategies while relying on community support during flooding events. However, challenges in resources and institutional support affected their ability to recover and prepare for future floods. These findings highlight the need for improved disaster preparedness, accessible health services, and stronger community support to promote public health and resilience in flood-prone areas.

title: “We Felt This Tether to the Hospital”: Lessons From the 2025 Los Angeles Wildfires for Climate‐Era Disaster Preparedness in Pediatric Cancer Care
abstract: INTRODUCTION: The January 2025 Los Angeles wildfires were among the most destructive disasters in California's history, displacing thousands of densely populated communities. Pediatric cancer patients represent a vulnerable population, as their interrupted treatment, immunocompromised status, and dependence on specialized care create compounding risks during disasters. This qualitative investigation examines the impact of the wildfires on pediatric cancer patients or survivors, their caregivers, and clinicians. METHODS: We conducted in-depth interviews (n = 13) with caregivers of children in active treatment or survivorship for cancer affected by the wildfires and focus group discussions with pediatric cancer care clinicians (n = 9) serving fire-impacted and at-risk communities. Thematic analysis was performed. RESULTS: Five themes captured how the wildfires disrupted pediatric cancer care and created intersecting burdens for caregivers and clinicians alike: (1) treatment disruptions, delays, and stressors; (2) concerns about healthcare access and hospital proximity in evacuation decisions; (3) gaps in timely and responsive communication; (4) compounding challenges for clinicians navigating personal wildfire impacts while delivering care; and (5) health system coordination, preparedness, and lessons learned. CONCLUSIONS: The wildfires exposed major gaps in how health systems support pediatric cancer patients during climate disasters. To improve resilience, health systems must invest in cross-institutional coordination, condition-specific clinical guidance, and communicate proactively with families before and during disasters. Future research should examine environmental hazard effects in medically vulnerable children and track longitudinal outcomes following care disruptions. Resilience in pediatric cancer care cannot be built in the aftermath of a disaster; it must be cultivated deliberately in the periods between them.

title: Beyond Flood Relief: An Integrated Socio-Ecological Framework for Biodiversity and Livelihood Resilience in Flood-Prone Agricultural Landscapes of India
abstract: Flooding in India is more than just a recurring natural hazard; it is a complex disruption thatdeeply impacts agricultural production, biodiversity, and rural livelihoods. Traditionally,flood management has focused on emergency response, financial relief, and infrastructurerepair. However, this reactive approach often overlooks the vital, interconnected ecologicaland economic factors that drive long-term recovery. To address this, we propose anIntegrated Socio-Ecological Framework for Biodiversity and Livelihood Resilience in Flood-Prone Agricultural Landscapes of India. This approach is built on the reality that farmingcommunities, local ecosystems, and rural economies depend entirely on one another. To buildtrue landscape-scale resilience, the framework integrates nine key dimensions: flood-riskassessment, ecosystem and wetland restoration, biodiversity conservation, climate-resilientagriculture, livelihood diversification, indigenous and community knowledge, early-warningsystems and digital technologies, participatory governance, and adaptive monitoring andlearning. Rather than simply bouncing back after a disaster, this study views flood resilienceas the ongoing ability to anticipate, adapt, and regenerate. We emphasize how naturaldefenses—such as wetlands, healthy soil biodiversity, and connected landscapes—caneffectively complement engineered flood barriers. Crucially, this framework reframes farmersnot merely as disaster victims, but as vital stewards of ecological recovery. By bridging thegap between biodiversity conservation and agricultural sustainability, this paper argues for anecessary shift: moving away from a relief-centric model toward a proactive strategy thatempowers India's flood-prone regions to withstand and adapt to a changing climate.

title: Perceived stress and social determinants of health among medical students in an earthquake-affected province: a stratified cross-sectional study
abstract: Background This study was conducted to examine the relationship between perceived stress at the medical school and the social determinants of health among medical students in Malatya, one of the provinces most severely affected by the earthquakes that struck Turkey on February 6, 2023. Methods A stratified cross-sectional study was conducted among 314 medical students at the Faculty of Medicine, İnönü University. Data were gathered through a sociodemographic information form, the Perceived Medical School Stress Scale (PMSS), and the Social Determinants of Health Scale for University Students (SDHUS). Student’s t-test and one-way ANOVA were applied for between-group comparisons, Pearson and Spearman correlation analyses for inter-scale relationships, and multivariable linear regression, with age entered as a continuous variable, to identify factors independently associated with PMSS and SDHUS total scores. Results The survey was completed by 314 of 339 eligible students (response rate 92.6%). In bivariate analyses, clinical-phase students, female students, students aged ≥ 22 years, and those residing independently had significantly higher PMSS total scores. In multivariable analysis, being in the clinical phase (B = 4.853; p < 0.001) and alcohol use (B = 3.160; p = 0.017) were independently associated with higher PMSS scores, whereas higher income level (B = − 4.293; p < 0.001), stronger peer support (B = − 2.429; p = 0.002), and regular physical activity (B = − 2.016; p = 0.028) were independently associated with lower PMSS scores; direct earthquake exposure showed a borderline association (B = 2.553; p = 0.045). The model accounted for 28.6% of the variance in PMSS total scores (adjusted R²=0.286). In the SDHUS model, bereavement (B = 1.697; p < 0.001) and clinical phase (B = 1.068; p = 0.015) were independently associated with greater social health needs. Students who had directly experienced the earthquake, sustained home damage, or lost a relative had significantly higher PMSS total scores in bivariate comparisons. Conclusions In this post-disaster setting, perceived stress among medical students was associated not only with academic factors but also with social determinants such as living conditions, income level, sleep quality, peer support, and exposure to the earthquake. These findings underscore the importance of comprehensive and targeted mental health interventions in post-disaster medical education, while acknowledging that the cross-sectional design does not permit causal inference.

title: Emergency Medical Care: From Scene to Survival
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Emergency Medical Care: From the Scene to SurvivalEmergency medicine is an important part of the health care system, emphasizing the rapid diagnosis, evaluation, stabilization and treatment of patients with acute illness, injury or life-threatening conditions. In an emergency situation every second counts and the correct medical intervention can be the difference between life and death. The burden of severe health conditions such as cardiovascular diseases, respiratory emergencies, infectious diseases, natural disasters, and road traffic accidents is growing and the importance of a properly organized and efficient emergency medical care system is becoming increasingly evident. The book Emergency Medical Care: From Scene to Survival is formulated to provide a thorough understanding of the contemporary methods, clinical practices, and basic principles that are critical to emergency health care. It is designed to give the reader a full understanding of the whole emergency management process from the initial scene assessment and the prehospital response to hospital-based treatment, critical care, rehabilitation and long-term patient recovery.The book is divided into twenty chapters that cover the major fields of emergency medical practice. It begins with a review of emergency medical care, including emergency scene assessment, patient evaluation, triage, basic life support and cardiopulmonary resuscitation techniques. It also covers airway management, respiratory and cardiovascular emergencies, shock, hemorrhage, trauma management, wound care, burns, neurological disorders, poisoning and environmental emergencies.Special attention is given to pediatric and neonatal emergencies, obstetric and gynecologic emergencies, geriatric emergencies, and the management of patients requiring specialized health care support. Also included are topics on prehospital emergency care, ambulance operations, emergency department management, intensive care support, disaster medicine, mass casualty management, psychological emergencies, therapeutic communication and ethical responsibilities.The final chapters focus on the need for post-emergency care, rehabilitation, patient safety, quality improvement, technological innovations and future advances in emergency medical services. Through these topics, readers are presented with the importance of patient-centered healthcare, inter-disciplinary coordination, evidence-based practices, and continuity of care.This book is designed for undergraduate and postgraduate students, nursing students, paramedical and allied health science students, emergency medical technicians, healthcare professionals, educators and those interested in emergency healthcare management. The content is organized in a systematic and educational manner to facilitate conceptual understanding, academic learning, and professional development.This book aims to increase awareness of the basic concepts of clinical decision- making, teamwork, timely intervention, effective communication and rapid assessment. It also emphasizes the value of patient dignity, safety, professional ethics and compassion when providing emergency care.The field of emergency medicine is changing with the development of medical technology, diagnostic tools, telemedicine, artificial intelligence and integrated emergency response systems. Therefore, adherence to updated clinical guidelines, hands-on training, and continuous learning will be crucial in improving healthcare outcomes and patient survival.This book is sincerely hoped to be a valuable educational and professional reference, increasing the knowledge and understanding of emergency medical care by healthcare practitioners and students. The ultimate goal is to help foster responsible, compassionate, and skilled healthcare practitioners in dealing with emergencies and helping patients transition from the scene to survival.

title: ORGANIZATIONAL PERFORMANCE AND EFFECTIVENESS: AN ORGANIZATIONAL DIAGNOSIS OF LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNIT A
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This study assessed the organizational performance and effectiveness of Local Government Unit A (LGU A), a component city in Region IV-A (CALABARZON), and proposed organizational development (OD) interventions to align its internal organizational health with its external competitive performance. It examined the city’s performance on the five pillars of the Cities and Municipalities Competitiveness Index (CMCI), employees’ perceptions on the seven dimensions of the Organizational Diagnosis Questionnaire (ODQ) anchored in Weisbord’s Six-Box Model, and the alignment between the two using Spearman rank correlation. Using a quantitative descriptive design, data were drawn from six years (2019–2024) of CMCI records and an ODQ survey of a stratified target sample of 317 respondents, drawn from 1,528 employees and comprising managers, supervisors, and rank-and-file employees. Competitiveness peaked in 2020 and declined in four of five pillars by 2024, with strengths in disaster preparedness, cost competitiveness, and investment promotion offset by weak road infrastructure, limited business group participation, and gaps in compliance and recognition systems; only Innovation improved consistently. Employees rated all seven ODQ dimensions favorably, with every item returning a median of Agree, though culturally shaped responses on participation, conflict, and rewards warrant attention. All 48 correlation pairs were significant, with Structure and Helpful Mechanisms most closely associated with external performance, yet the dominant pattern is divergence: a healthy internal climate alongside external decline. Eight OD interventions are proposed to mobilize this internal strength toward competitive recovery.

title: Fractional CO₂ laser for eyelid and periorbital wrinkles and laxity: short- and long-term clinical results using a standardized protocol
abstract: Objective Eyelid and periorbital rejuvenation is a common aesthetic concern. This study aimed to describe an original and detailed fractional CO₂ laser protocol and evaluate its efficacy and safety for skin tightening and wrinkle reduction in the upper and lower eyelids and periorbital region, with 12-month follow-up. Materials and Methods A single-arm, evaluator-blinded clinical trial was conducted in 27 patients presenting with eyelid and periorbital laxity and wrinkles. All patients underwent a single session of fractional CO₂ laser treatment. Clinical outcomes were assessed at 3, 6, and 12 months using two study-specific grading scales evaluated by two independent expert assessors, along with patient-reported outcomes. Results Significant reductions were observed in eyelid and periorbital laxity (p < 0.0001) and in fine lines and wrinkle depth (p < 0.0001). At 3 months, 74% of patients achieved good overall improvement (50–75% correction; p < 0.0001). Improvements were maintained over time with minor variations, including a peak effect at 6 months followed by a slight decline at 12 months. At 12 months, 70% of patients reported being satisfied or very satisfied. No unexpected adverse events or complications were observed. Conclusion The protocol described appears to be a safe and potentially effective approach for eyelid and periorbital rejuvenation, associated with improvements in skin tightening and wrinkle reduction, with high patient satisfaction and results generally maintained over at least a 12-month follow-up.

title: Integrating artificial intelligence, internet of things, big data analytics within digital twins for resilient supply chains: current contributions, challenges and future pathways
abstract: Amid increasing global disruptions and uncertainty, supply chain resilience (SCRES) has become a critical strategic priority. Although intelligent digital twins, powered by underlying Industry 4.0 technologies, are widely recognized as important enablers of resilient supply chains, existing research offers a limited understanding of how specific technological integrations strengthen SCRES capabilities. To address this gap, this state-of-the-art review examines how the Internet of Things (IoT), Big Data Analytics (BDA), and Artificial Intelligence (AI) act as foundational layers integrated within digital twins for enhancing SCRES. Using a PRISMA-guided review and a Group Technology-inspired clustering approach, the study identifies distinct technology–resilience integration patterns that explain how these technologies jointly support resilience capabilities such as agility, flexibility, robustness, collaboration, and visibility. The findings reveal that resilience emerges not from decomposed technologies, but from the synergistic integration with digital twins. Specifically, IoT-driven integrations primarily enhance visibility, prediction, and agility through real time sensing and rapid response mechanisms, while BDA-centered integrations strengthen robustness and collaboration through data-driven decision making and system insights. AI-enabled digital twins further support adaptive and proactive resilience through predictive analytics, intelligent scenario evaluation, and dynamic decision support. Despite these benefits, key implementation challenges remain, including interoperability issues, cybersecurity risks, high implementation costs, and limited empirical validation. This study contributes to the literature by moving beyond fragmented technology-centric perspectives toward a structured understanding of how integrated digital twins with IoT, AI, and BDA generate SCRES. The proposed synthesis provides both theoretical insights and practical guidance for researchers and practitioners.

title: Editorial: Italian cities in transition: a critical assessment of socio-ecological change
abstract: Since the '80s, a large body of research has positioned cities, particularly large metropolitan areas, at the heart of wealth creation processes associated with the knowledge economy and globalized capitalism. Different lines of research have examined cities as hubs of development and innovation, as places where leadership and control functions are concentrated, and as pivotal nodes of flows and centers of accumulation in contemporary financial and technological capitalism. This body of work has given rise to the notion of global urban development (Theodore and Peck, 2024), which is based on the idea that cities are primarily engines of growth and that globalization is fundamentally an urban phenomenon. Optimistic and celebratory accounts of the city as a magnet for the creative class and as a cluster of innovative activities have, in turn, informed urban policies aimed at enhancing competitiveness and attractiveness (Pinson, 2020). Similarly, although the original global city model drew attention to processes of social polarization, subsequent debate surrounding this model has fostered public and political reflection on promoting cities within the global economy (Le Galès, 2024). Rankings based on indicators of connectivity and integration into global markets as well as an emphasis on cities' capacity to create conditions conducive to capital accumulation have fostered the diffusion of public policies that aim to improve cities' positions within the urban hierarchy and enhance their attractiveness to flows of capital, investment, and highly skilled professionals. Although not all cities have the status and influence of global metropolises, urban studies have reported the widespread adoption of city-building policies that promote investment and market development as well as position every city as a global city (Le Galès, 2024). Urban marketing and the organization of cultural events are considered key components of city branding. This reflects a growing connection between entrepreneurial urbanism (Harvey, 1989) and globalization (Le Galès, 2024), as well as a gradual shift in public policy from demand-side to supply-side approaches (Pinson, 2020). While critical urban studies have sometimes overstated the ubiquity and power of this market-oriented trend (Pinson, 2020), there is a general agreement that this phase of urban policymaking has led to urban transformations largely centered on the valorization of specific neighborhoods, particularly central urban areas. This often results in processes of spatial segregation, gentrification and displacement. In less developed regions, where growth prospects in advanced economic sectors are relatively limited -as is often the case in Southern European cities -the functional reorganization of historic centers is also seen as a public strategy to attract tourists (Estevens et al., 2023).Recently, however, the scientific debate on cities has turned its attention to the darker side of marketdriven development. Even scholars who once advocated for strengthening cities' competitive advantages now acknowledge that urban development strategies based on attractiveness and competition can have destructive consequences. Rising rents and property costs have reached levels that are unsustainable for many residents (Florida, 2017). Peripheral areas, territories, and people left behind by the economic accumulation processes of the first phase of globalization are receiving renewed attention (Rodríguez-Pose et al., 2023). A novel perspective on capitalist dynamics places the quality of everyday life and citizens' well-being at its core, challenging the notion that these can depend solely on wealth accumulation (Foundational Economy Collective, 2018). From this point of view, the selective and exclusive effects of urban transformations driven by policies promoting attractiveness and competitiveness are much more visible and open to critical scrutiny. Not least, as the climate crisis emerges as one of the defining challenges of our time, a new research agenda on the urban transitions is emerging (Le Galès, 2024). International frameworks such as the United Nations' 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (SDG 11), the New Urban Agenda, and the European Green Deal all recognize cities as key players in the pursuit of the ecological transition.However, sustainability policies are not neutral: they may generate new inequalities between social groups and territories (Rodríguez-Pose and Bartalucci, 2024). Cities are therefore increasingly expected to ensure that the transition proceeds in a just and inclusive manner, avoiding the production of new social and spatial disparities. From this perspective, environmental sustainability, social cohesion, and social inclusion are conceived to be mutually reinforcing objectives rather than competing priorities. There is a clear and close connection between the research agenda that focuses on how cities ensure a satisfactory quality of life for their citizens and the agenda that examines cities' capacity to pursue sustainability goals. Accordingly to the widely accepted definition, sustainability is the ability to meet current needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs. This approach involves striking a balance between environmental protection, social inclusion, and long-term economic development. Thus, both strands of urban research, therefore, prioritize citizens' wellbeing, address inequalities, and promote the responsible use of resources. Instead of emphasizing the promotion of immediate economic growth, they focus on the capacity of cities and urban policies to achieve long-term development objectives without generating territorial imbalances or excessive dependence on a single sector, such as tourism.This special issue contributes to the ongoing debate by focusing on Italian cities. These cities have not been studied much, but they provide a suitable context for reflecting on these topics. First, much like the urban systems in Europe more broadly, the Italian urban system is characterized by a widespread network of cities, in which small-and medium-sized urban centers play a significant role alongside larger metropolitan areas. Second, territorial disparities between the north and south persist, resulting in different opportunities for promoting sustainability across cities. Furthermore, Italian municipalities have been assigned a central role in implementing the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR), one of Europe's most ambitious policy initiatives. Finally, the urgency of sustainability challenges is especially evident in Italy: between 2020 and 2025, the number of extreme weather events increased by 53%foot_0 , with substantial economic consequences. According to the European Environment Agencyfoot_1 , Italy currently ranks second in Europe for economic losses caused by climate-related disasters, amounting to over €145 billion between 1980 and 2025. At the time these pages were written, an unprecedented heatwave was unfolding, with temperatures reaching levels never before recorded globally in the ERA5 dataset, according to the Copernicus Climate Change Service. Italy was among the European regions most severely affected by temperature anomalies.A national research program (GC-LIFESGC-LIFES. Grounded cities. Liveability, Foundational Economy and urban Space of cities in the middle) is theoretically informed by the Foundational Economy perspective and empirically centered on "intermediate cities". It offers a compelling illustration of the shift in focus within urban studies. The project comprises three contributions to this research topic that address distinct dimensions of urban life and change and are closely related and complementary. These contributions are united by a common concern: understanding how the quality of urban life is produced, experienced, and threatened in contemporary cities. Bozzon, Arcidiacono, Avola, Ebbreo, and Cabria (2026) address this issue by focusing on the concept of liveability. They free this concept from its traditionally subordinate role within the paradigm of the competitive and attractive city. They re-establish it as an autonomous analytical category and as a social and environmental objective within a conception of the city centered on residents' quality of life. Drawing on data from official statistical sources, the authors examine approximately one hundred provincial capital municipalities across the diverse landscape of the Italian urban system. In this context, medium-sized cities emerge as a distinct urban configuration in terms of liveability. They resemble larger cities in terms of income levels and essential services yet display social infrastructure more akin to smaller cities. However, this differentiation remains along the country's North-South divide. The first contribution examines liveability using objective indicators, while the second considers how citizens perceive it. Podda, Cabria, and Zurru (2026) provide a thorough theoretical discussion of the Foundational Economy framework, forming the basis of a research strategy. Its empirical component draws on survey data collected in three medium-sized cities in southern Italy. The results show that the quality of urban life is shaped by the interplay between territorial context and socioeconomic conditions. The city predominantly influences the quality of available infrastructure and services, neighborhoods affect the accessibility of local services and social infrastructure, and income levels determine individuals' ability to access these services. Consequently, different combinations of citylevel context, neighborhood characteristics, and individual economic conditions result in unequal opportunities in using services and experiencing urban well-being. Whereas the first two contributions focus on liveability and its determinants, the third examines how recent urban transformations have threatened it. Salento, Corrado, Ebbreo, Latronico, Podda, and Saiu (2026) examine the processes of real-estate valorization associated with these transformations. Allthough these transformations have traditionally been interpreted through the lens of gentrification, the authors use a more appropriate framework to capture the specific characteristics of medium-sized cities. Through a comparative analysis of three urban contexts and employing a mixed-methods approach, the authors show that the extraction of value associated with the transformation of historic city centers for tourism, commerce, and leisure occurs through changes in land use, even without residential displacement. These processes are therefore better understood through the concept of urban rent than through gentrification. Nevertheless, they remain selective and exclusionary. In the absence of adequate regulatory measures, they contribute to the erosion of the fundamental pillars of the liveability for resident citizens. Together, the three articles provide an important contextual framework for analyzing transitions toward sustainable development. In Italy, recent urban transformations in medium-sized cities, as well as in other urban contexts, have largely been driven by broad social coalitions seeking to increase the valorization of private real estate. Without effective public regulation, these processes may undermine collective well-being, while generating tensions with the social and environmental sustainability of urban development. Against this backdrop, some crucial questions arise: how do socio-ecological transitions emerge? Which actors drive them, and through which governance arrangements?Cities are not merely places of exploitation and exclusion; they are also laboratories for experimentation, testing new actors, governance arrangements, and economic practices. The articles in this collection address the question of who is leading the alternative paths toward socio-ecological transition and the governance arrangements though which they are leading. The articles highlight three interconnected dimensions: the actors involved, the institutional frameworks through which action is organized, and the conditions that support or constrain change.pag. 4The first dimension concerns the actors involved in shaping urban transitions. Public authorities, civil society organizations, hybrid enterprises, and citizens are key actors that shape socio-ecological change in different ways and with different capacities. Public authorities, often considered the primary drivers of urban transition, can both enable and constrain transformative processes. Bergonzini, Calori, Minotti, Giordano, Volpe, Defili, and Petruzzella's (2026) mapping of Italian food governance initiatives reveals that municipalities are the most common project leaders, with more than 70 percent of initiatives involving public administrations in some capacity. This confirms the central role of city governments in advancing sustainability agendas, in line with international frameworks such as the Milan Urban Food Policy Pact. However, the authors also note that municipal leadership can result in longer implementation times and reduced flexibility, highlighting the ambivalent effects of institutionalization.
