Epidemiology of serious bacterial infections among hospitalised children aged <5 years in eastern Ethiopia
journal: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine
abstract: Background: Serious bacterial infections (SBIs), particularly bacteraemia, remain a primary driver of global paediatric mortality, accounting for nearly 20% of the five million deaths in children aged <5 years in 2019. In low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), paediatric bacteraemia case fatality risks (CFR) range from 12.0% to 28.0%, compared with 6.0-14% in high-income countries (HICs). In eastern Ethiopia, limited local microbiological granular data constrain evidence-based management of paediatric SBIs and monitoring of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Methods: This thesis mainly utilised prospective hospital-based clinical surveillance complemented by a secondary analysis of post-mortem data. Between December 2021 and November 2023, I co-established and led the Invasive Bacterial Disease (IBD) surveillance platform at Hiwot Fana Comprehensive Specialised Hospital (HFCSH) in eastern Ethiopia, enrolling all children aged <5 years admitted for acute care; excluding elective surgery and acute poisonings. For this PhD thesis, analyses were restricted to blood cultures collected within 48 hours of admission to capture presumed community-acquired bacteraemia. Neonates (0–28 completed days) meeting clinical world health organization (WHO) possible SBI (pSBI), and children aged 1–59 months with clinical syndromes suggestive of SBI (including pneumonia, meningitis) and non-SBI acute admissions were included. Demographic, clinical, microbiological, and in-hospital outcome data were collected to determine bacteraemia proportions and in-hospital deaths, and to identify associated factors. Isolates were identified using API kits and antimicrobial susceptibility was tested by Kirby-Bauer methods following standard laboratory procedures. To assess the bacteraemia diagnostic yield, I compared the results of paired blood culture and PCR assays from blood samples collected via subclavian vein shortly after death from stillbirths and children aged <5 years enrolled in the Child Health and Mortality Prevention Surveillance (CHAMPS)–Ethiopia programme (September 2019 December 2024). Most of these post-mortem blood specimens (87.1%, 853/979) were collected within 24 hours of death. This secondary analysis was designed to compare the relative sensitivity of bacterial and fungal pathogen detection by culture and PCR, not to estimate absolute diagnostic accuracy. Results: Among 3,290 eligible hospitalised children aged <5 years, culture-confirmed bacteraemia was identified in 592 (18.0%). Overall CFR was 18.8% (111/592), including 22.5% (80/356) in neonates with pSBI and 13.1% (31/236) in children aged 1-59 months. Among 1,535 admitted neonates, 1,375 met WHO pSBI criteria. Blood cultures were collected from 1,335, and after excluding 115 potential contaminants, 29.2% (356/1,220) had bacteraemia. Neonates with pSBI had higher bacteraemia proportion (29.2% vs.11.4%, p<0.001) and associated CFR (22.5% vs.13.1%, p<0.001) than children aged 1–59 months. Among neonates with pSBI, Pantoea dispersa (n=145,40.7%) and Klebsiella pneumoniae (n=63,17.7%) were predominant. The CFR among monomicrobial P. dispersa infections was 25.0% (32/128). In 2,366 children aged 1–59 months admitted for acute care, 11.4% (236/2,070) had a positive cultures after excluding contaminants (n=296), and 11.2% (58/516) were non-SBI cases. Klebsiella oxytoca (n=59,25.0%) was the predominant pathogen. Klebsiella species exhibited high resistance to antibiotics included in WHO-recommended first- and second-line treatment regimens. Conversely, P. dispersa was largely susceptible to gentamicin but demonstrated notable resistance to ampicillin and cefotaxime. Low birthweight (<2500 g) (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 2.1; 95% CI 1.2-3.5), admission in dry season (Oct-Jan) (aOR 9.7; 95% CI 4.6-20.3) compared to rainy season (Jun-Sept), and delivery outside HFCSH (aOR 1.9; 95% CI 1.2-3.0) were associated with P. dispersa associated bacteraemia, while severe wasting (aOR 1.5; 95% CI 1.1-2.0) was associated with bacteraemia in children aged 1–59 months. Bacteraemia was associated with increased risk of in-hospital death among neonates (adjusted risk ratio [aRR] 1.8; 95% CI 1.2-2.6) and children aged 1–59 months (aRR 5.6; 95% CI 2.9-10.8). Low birthweight (aRR 1.9; 95% CI 1.2-3.0) and severe wasting (aRR 4.1; 95% CI 2.6-6.6) were associated with in-hospital deaths. In post mortem analyses, pathogen detection varied by diagnostic method (interaction p< 0.001), with PCR detecting more S. pneumoniae (OR 41.0; 95% CI 5.6–298.1) and culture identifying more K. pneumoniae (OR 0.5, 95% CI 0.3–0.8). Conclusion: Bacteraemia was common among children aged < 5 years admitted for acute care to a referral hospital in eastern Ethiopia and was linked with high in-hospital mortality, especially among neonates. The hospital-based burden appeared to be shaped by upstream determinants, including low birthweight, place of delivery, and wasting. The predominance of P. dispersa associated neonatal bacteraemia, particularly among neonates born outside HFCSH, warrants further investigation into potential environmental, referralchain, and healthcare-associated transmission pathways. The observed association between neonatal bacteraemia and delivery outside HFCSH suggests that exposures occurring before admission may contribute to neonatal infection and highlights the need for exploration of infection prevention and control (IPC) practices, particularly across the referral network. Paired post-mortem results indicate that blood culture and molecular diagnostics provide complementary insights into SBI aetiology, while recognising that pathogen detection alone does not establish causation. Collectively, these results support strengthened microbiological surveillance to monitor pathogen distribution and AMR patterns, antimicrobial stewardship, and IPC practice. While this study was not aimed to evaluate the adequacy of specific empirical regimens, data may contribute to future evidence-based review of hospital-level empirical SBI management strategies in similar resource-limited settings. Future research may prioritise understanding the ecology and transmission routes of rarely described pathogens, including P. dispersa.

title: Current awareness and influencing factors regarding digital out-of-hospital health monitoring among patients after gastrointestinal surgery: A cross-sectional study
abstract: BACKGROUND Postoperative patients in gastrointestinal surgery often face interrupted professional care and insufficient rehabilitation guidance after discharge. Digital out-of-hospital health monitoring can provide remote monitoring and abnormality alerts, yet its effectiveness depends on patients' adequate cognition of the service. Currently, there is a lack of research on the cognitive status and influencing factors in this population. AIM To investigate the cognitive status of digital out-of-hospital health monitoring among postoperative patients in gastrointestinal surgery and analyze its influencing factors. METHODS A convenience sampling method was used to select 126 postoperative patients discharged from the gastrointestinal surgery department of a tertiary hospital. A self-designed cognitive questionnaire (4 dimensions, 15 items, Likert 5-point scale) was administered. A t test, analysis of variance, and multiple linear regression were used to analyze influencing factors. RESULTS The mean item score of cognition among the 126 patients was (3.02 ± 0.43), indicating a moderately low level. The value cognition dimension scored the highest, while the concern cognition dimension scored the lowest. Univariate analysis showed that age, education level, years of smartphone use, and health app use experience significantly affected the total cognitive score (all P < 0.05). Multiple regression analysis revealed that years of smartphone use (β = 0.203) and health app use experience (β = -0.176) were independent influencing factors. CONCLUSION Postoperative patients in gastrointestinal surgery exhibit generally low cognition of digital out-of-hospital health monitoring, characterized by a "value recognition preceding basic cognition" pattern and prevalent concerns. Digital contact experience predicts cognitive level better than demographic characteristics. Stratified health education should be implemented to strengthen service concept awareness, while technical optimization should be adopted to alleviate patient concerns.

title: Readiness for transition to adult-oriented care among adolescents with cancer and sickle cell disease at the Uganda Cancer Institute: a cross-sectional study
abstract: Background The transition from paediatric to adult-oriented healthcare requires adolescents with chronic conditions to develop skills for independent self-management and engagement with healthcare providers. Empirical data on transition readiness among adolescents with cancer or sickle cell disease (SCD) in Uganda are lacking. We assessed transition readiness and its associated factors among adolescents with cancer or SCD at the Uganda Cancer Institute (UCI). Methods We conducted a cross-sectional study among 70 adolescents aged 15 to <18 years with cancer or SCD managed at UCI, recruited consecutively between 1 July and 30 August 2026. Transition readiness was assessed using the 20-item Transition Readiness Assessment Questionnaire (TRAQ), covering medication management, appointment keeping, tracking health issues, and communication with healthcare providers. A composite score (range 1–5) was calculated as the mean across the four domains, with higher scores indicating greater readiness. Scores were categorised as low (<3.375), moderate (3.375–3.90), adequate (3.91–4.70), or excellent (>4.70). Factors associated with composite scores were assessed using t-tests, ANOVA, and multiple linear regression. Results Mean age was 16.7 years (SD 1.1), and 41 (58.6%) were female. The mean composite TRAQ score was 3.27 (SD 0.80). Forty participants (57.1%) had low readiness and only 14 (20.0%) had adequate or excellent readiness. Communication with providers scored highest (mean 3.86), whereas medication management (3.07), keeping appointments (3.10), and tracking health issues (3.06) were markedly lower. The composite score was positively correlated with age (ρ =0.31, p = 0.008) and was higher in adolescents aged 17 to <18 years than in those aged 15 to 16 years (3.49 vs. 2.98; p = 0.005), and age was the only factor independently associated with the score (β =0.22 per year, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.41; p = 0.026). Only 25 participants (35.7%) reported that the clinical team had discussed transfer to adult services with them, and this was not associated with readiness. Conclusions Most adolescents had low transition readiness, particularly in medication management, appointment keeping, and tracking health issues, and scores were higher among older adolescents. These findings suggest that skills-based transition preparation within paediatric haematology and oncology care should be developed and evaluated; longitudinal studies are needed.
